* Xcode for iOS simulator and device automation (`simctl` and `devicectl`). `agent-device` uses the Xcode in `DEVELOPER_DIR`, otherwise the one from `xcode-select -p`. A `DEVELOPER_DIR` exported in the shell where you run `agent-device` applies to that command, even when a local daemon is already running; without it, the daemon uses the environment it started in. Set `DEVELOPER_DIR=""` to use the daemon host’s `xcode-select` selection instead.
* Android SDK and ADB for Android, Android TV, and Fire TV devices running Fire OS
* HarmonyOS Command Line Tools for HarmonyOS (`hdc` available through `HDC_SDK_PATH`, `DEVECO_SDK_HOME`, or `HARMONYOS_COMMAND_LINE_TOOLS`)
* Amazon Vega Developer Tools and an SDK-matched Vega Virtual Device for Vega OS TV
* Swift 5.9 or newer (Xcode command-line tools) for macOS desktop targets. `agent-device` builds its local macOS helper on first use

## Global install

```bash
npm install -g agent-device@latest
agent-device doctor
agent-device --version
agent-device help
```

Run `agent-device doctor` yourself after installing to check that local devices, toolchains, and dev servers are ready before you hand the CLI to an agent.

A global install gives agents a stable `agent-device` command. Start with the core workflow guide; [Commands](/docs/commands) lists the other help topics:

```bash
agent-device help workflow
```

For Cursor, Codex, Claude Code, Windsurf, Cline, Goose, skills, and project rules, see [AI agent setup](/docs/agent-setup); to expose commands as MCP tools with `agent-device mcp`, see [MCP server](/docs/agent-setup#mcp-server). If an agent can’t find `agent-device` after a global install, see [Fix a missing agent-device command](/docs/agent-setup#fix-a-missing-agent-device-command). For the first app automation commands, see [Quick start](/docs/quick-start).

## Update the CLI

Interactive CLI runs periodically check npm for a newer `agent-device` release in the background. When one is available, the CLI suggests reinstalling globally:

```bash
npm install -g agent-device@latest
agent-device doctor
agent-device --version
```

Set `AGENT_DEVICE_NO_UPDATE_NOTIFIER=1` to disable the notice.

## Nightly builds

Nightly builds publish `main` after its CI passes, at most once per UTC day:

```bash
npm install -g agent-device@nightly
```

A nightly install’s update notice recommends a newer nightly when an update check finds one. To return to stable releases, install `agent-device@latest`.

## Without installing

```bash
npx agent-device --version
npx agent-device help workflow
npx agent-device open Settings --platform ios
```

One-off `npx` use is fine for you and for scripts that intentionally fetch from npm. For agents, use a global install, a project-local install, or a version pinned by you or your project config, so repeated commands resolve to a known CLI. Don’t let agents choose a version or run `npx -y agent-device@latest` unless you’ve decided to trust whatever npm serves.

## Vega OS TV prerequisites

Install the Amazon Vega Developer Tools and a matching Vega SDK and Vega Virtual Device (VVD) with Amazon’s installer, then load its environment and verify the tools:

```bash
source ~/vega/env
vega --version
vega doctor
vega device list
```

* Start and stop the local emulator with `vega virtual-device start` and `vega virtual-device stop`; `agent-device` does not boot it implicitly.
* Appium is optional. You don’t need it for device discovery, app lifecycle, or remote-button control.
* For selecting the VVD and what Vega OS supports, see [TV targets](/docs/commands#tv-targets).

## Fire TV prerequisites

A Fire TV device or emulator that runs Fire OS (Android-based) needs no extra tooling: enable ADB debugging in Settings > My Fire TV > Developer options, connect over the network, and automate it as an Android TV device.

```bash
adb connect 192.168.1.20:5555
agent-device devices --platform android
agent-device open <package> --platform android --target tv
```

Some Fire TV devices ship with Vega OS instead of Fire OS. Vega OS is a different OS and is supported only in the Vega Virtual Device; see [Vega OS TV prerequisites](#vega-os-tv-prerequisites). For what a Fire TV gets on the Android TV backend, see [TV targets](/docs/commands#tv-targets).

## macOS desktop notes

* macOS desktop automation uses a local `agent-device-macos-helper` for permission checks (`settings permission ...`), alert handling, and the `frontmost-app`, `desktop`, and `menubar` snapshot surfaces.
* `agent-device` builds the helper on first use and after updates, and caches it under `~/.agent-device/macos-helper/current/`.
* To use your own helper build, set `AGENT_DEVICE_MACOS_HELPER_BIN` to its absolute executable path.

## iOS physical device prerequisites

Run `agent-device help physical-device` for the same setup guidance from the CLI.

* Xcode is installed with `xcrun devicectl` and `xcrun xctrace` available.

* The device is paired, trusted, connected, unlocked when needed, and listed by `xcrun devicectl list devices`. A paired device that CoreDevice cannot reach (`tunnelState: unavailable`, for example unplugged and off the network) is listed by `devices` with `booted: false`. Commands refuse it with `details.kind: not_ready` and `details.tunnelState: unavailable`.

* Developer Mode is on in the device’s Settings.

* The Apple runner must be signed before commands can run on the device. Start with Automatic Signing in Xcode and these environment variables; add the others below only when needed:

  * `AGENT_DEVICE_IOS_TEAM_ID`
  * `AGENT_DEVICE_IOS_BUNDLE_ID` (optional base bundle ID for the runner app; its tests use `<id>.uitests`)

* To find team IDs and Apple Development signing certificates, run `security find-identity -v -p codesigning`.

* If Xcode can’t choose a provisioning profile, set `AGENT_DEVICE_IOS_PROVISIONING_PROFILE` to the profile name, not a file path.

* Set `AGENT_DEVICE_IOS_SIGNING_IDENTITY` only when `xcodebuild` asks for a specific identity.

* The profile and team must allow both `AGENT_DEVICE_IOS_BUNDLE_ID` and `<id>.uitests`.

* Free Apple Developer (Personal Team) accounts can fail with “bundle identifier is not available” for generic IDs. Set `AGENT_DEVICE_IOS_BUNDLE_ID` to a unique reverse-DNS value (for example `com.yourname.agentdevice.runner`).

* When the runner fails to start, `error.details.reason` is one of `signing_no_development_team`, `signing_provisioning_profile_missing`, `bundle_identifier_already_registered`, `signing_unspecified`, `devtools_security_developer_mode_disabled` (the Mac’s `DevToolsSecurity` setting, which says nothing about the device’s Developer Mode toggle), `simulator_service_hub_unavailable`, `simulator_set_destination_not_found` (a `--ios-simulator-device-set` simulator the selected Xcode cannot resolve, which names the set), `device_developer_mode_disabled`, `device_developer_disk_image_unavailable`, or `build_failed_unclassified` when the cause is unknown. Branch on `details.reason` and follow `hint`; the error code is `COMMAND_FAILED` for every reason.

* `simulator_service_hub_unavailable` means the selected Xcode is too old for the host macOS: macOS refuses to load that Xcode’s `DTServiceHub`, so every iOS Simulator runner start fails. Commands the runner doesn’t serve keep working — `open`, and a `snapshot` or `screenshot` the simulator bridge answers — while a capture the runner has to serve (`snapshot --actions`, `snapshot --observe-only`, or one the bridge can’t answer) fails the same way. The `DTServiceHub` refusal is visible in `runner.log`. Fix it on the machine running the daemon: `xcode-select -s /Applications/Xcode.app`, or start the daemon with `DEVELOPER_DIR=/Applications/Xcode.app`, pointing at an Xcode that supports this macOS. The command fails as soon as the refusal reaches `runner.log` instead of waiting out the connect timeout, and the failure is not retried or rebuilt, because neither can change which Xcode the host can load.

* The two `device_*` reasons come from the device itself (`xcrun devicectl device info details`), checked before the runner builds. `device_developer_mode_disabled` means the Developer Mode toggle in Settings is off; turn it on. `device_developer_disk_image_unavailable` means Developer Mode is on but the developer disk image isn’t available yet, usually because device support is still installing; wait and retry.

* The first run builds the Apple runner and takes longer than later commands. Keep the device connected; if setup times out, retry with `--debug` to see signing and build diagnostics.

* If you set `AGENT_DEVICE_IOS_RUNNER_DERIVED_PATH` together with `AGENT_DEVICE_IOS_CLEAN_DERIVED`, keep the path in a subdirectory of the project’s `.tmp/` directory. For any other path, the command fails instead of cleaning it, and the error hint names both fixes.

## Troubleshoot daemon startup and upgrades

If the daemon fails to start, retry with `--debug` and check the state directory and diagnostics. `agent-device session state-dir` prints the resolved directory without starting a daemon.

Before you upgrade from a version that predates the current daemon lock format, stop every older client and daemon that uses the state directory, using their original CLI. Don’t let older versions restart while the upgraded version runs. To run several versions at once, give each its own environment and state directory.

If you ran a source checkout from before state directories were per worktree, stop its daemon in `~/.agent-device` from that older checkout:

```sh
AGENT_DEVICE_STATE_DIR="$HOME/.agent-device" pnpm clean:daemon
```

An upgraded checkout uses a different default directory, so a plain `pnpm clean:daemon` there doesn’t reach the old daemon.

The daemon refuses to start when it finds a legacy lock file or can’t verify who owns the state directory. Before you recover manually, confirm that every client and daemon using the directory has stopped. Deleting `daemon.json` or `daemon.lock` alone is not a safe reset.

Packaged installs use `~/.agent-device` by default; source checkouts use a per-worktree directory under `~/.agent-device/dev/`. Set `AGENT_DEVICE_STATE_DIR` or pass `--state-dir` to override either default. Keep that directory private to your own account: it holds the daemon’s record, log, and recordings, so agent-device refuses to use one another account owns or can write, or one that is a symbolic link. [Supported environment variables](/docs/configuration#supported-environment-variables) states what a state directory must look like and how to fix one.

In a source checkout, `pnpm clean:daemon --prune-dev` first stops the current checkout’s daemon; the 14-day inactivity rule below does not apply to it. It then finds development state directories with no activity for 14 days (by the newest modification time of the directory and its immediate children) and removes daemon registrations it can confirm are abandoned. It keeps the directories, session artifacts, and logs.

# Introduction

> Learn what agent-device is, where it fits in agentic mobile, TV, desktop, and web development, and how agents use it for app verification, debugging, profiling, QA, and replay.

`agent-device` is an open source device layer for coding agents: a CLI, MCP server, and Node.js API that let agents verify and QA apps, locally or in device clouds, on iOS, Android, HarmonyOS, tvOS, watchOS simulators, Android TV, Fire TV devices running Fire OS, Amazon Vega OS TV apps in the Vega Virtual Device, macOS (including Electron apps), Linux desktop targets, and a limited managed web browser. Which interactions, structured UI, evidence, performance, and replay features you get depends on what each target supports.

Use it when an agent needs to inspect and operate a running app, not only reason about source code or screenshots.

`agent-device` operates the app and collects evidence. It does not decide what to test: your coding agent, QA agent, or project harness reads the task, interprets the current screen, chooses commands, and judges whether the result meets the scenario. Because decisions stay with the agent, you can mix live exploration, deterministic replay, and human review.

## What you can use it for

* **App verification for agents**: run the app, inspect visible UI, act through refs/selectors, and verify expected state.
* **Token-efficient UI context**: accessibility snapshots give agents structured UI state instead of screenshots alone.
* **Runtime evidence**: capture screenshots, recordings, logs, network traffic, audio-level probes for browser and host-rendered simulator/emulator audio, traces, CPU/memory/perf snapshots, and crash-related logs when the happy path breaks.
* **Replayable checks**: turn stable exploratory sessions into `.ad` replay scripts that run again without AI.
* **React Native and Expo workflows**: pair device automation with React component inspection and performance profiling that names slow renders, rerenders, and their causes.
* **Local devices and app surfaces**: drive simulators, emulators, physical devices, TV targets, desktop apps, and browser sessions through one CLI.

If you know `agent-browser`, `agent-device` brings the same workflow to mobile, TV, desktop, and a limited managed web browser.

## Development loop

With `agent-device`, an agent can write code, run the app, verify the UI end to end, collect screenshots, videos, logs, and performance evidence, and feed bugs, crashes, or performance findings into the next fix before a human reviews the PR.

![Sketch showing agent-device as the live app verification layer in the agentic development loop](/agentic-development-loop.svg)

## How agents use it

A typical session looks like this:

```bash
agent-device apps --platform ios
agent-device open <app-or-url> --platform ios
agent-device snapshot -i
agent-device press @e12
agent-device diff snapshot -i
agent-device close
```

Snapshots come from the accessibility tree: labels, roles, values, and test IDs are what agents use to choose refs and selectors. Screenshots and videos remain useful as evidence and as a fallback when a screen exposes poor accessibility data, but refs and selectors are more reliable than pixel or OCR guesses.

Start with the core workflow guide in the installed CLI help. [Commands](/docs/commands) lists the other help topics, which agents read for specialized work or when a command is unclear:

```bash
agent-device help workflow
```

Use [AI agent setup](/docs/agent-setup) for Cursor, Codex, Claude Code, Windsurf, Cline, Goose, skills, and MCP setup. Use [Commands](/docs/commands) for detailed command groups and platform behavior.

## Where it fits

`agent-device` is for agents, but humans still install it, grant permissions, review artifacts, and decide what ships.

For stable, repeatable test suites, use [e2e](https://e2e.com/), a TypeScript testing framework for web and mobile apps. Use `agent-device` when an agent needs to explore, reproduce, debug, profile, collect evidence, or record a replay from live app behavior.

MCP clients can drive devices directly through the `agent-device mcp` server, which exposes the installed commands as structured tools. See [MCP server](/docs/agent-setup#mcp-server).

## Next steps

* Install the CLI: [Installation](/docs/installation)
* Set up an agent client: [AI agent setup](/docs/agent-setup)
* Run the first commands: [Quick start](/docs/quick-start)
* Inspect all command groups: [Commands](/docs/commands)
* Collect runtime evidence: [Debugging and profiling](/docs/debugging-profiling)
* Record deterministic flows: [Replay and E2E testing](/docs/replay-e2e)

# Known limitations

Platform constraints that change what you see during automation, and what to do instead.

## iOS: “Allow Paste” dialog never appears

iOS 16+ shows an “Allow Paste” system prompt when an app reads `UIPasteboard.general` in the foreground. When `agent-device` launches or activates an iOS app, it does so through the Apple runner (an XCUITest runner), and iOS silently grants pasteboard access in that context, so the prompt never appears.

This Apple platform constraint affects every XCUITest-based automation tool.

**Workarounds:**

* **Pre-fill the pasteboard** with the text the app will read, before it reads:

  ```bash
  agent-device clipboard write "some text" --platform ios --udid <simulator-udid>
  ```

* **Test the dialog manually.** XCUITest-based automation cannot exercise the “Allow Paste” UX.

## iOS simulator: `simctl pbcopy` writes nothing under Xcode 27

Under Xcode 27, `xcrun simctl pbcopy <udid>` exits 0 but leaves the simulator’s pasteboard empty. `simctl pbinfo` then lists a `Promised` item that reads back empty.

Use `agent-device clipboard write` instead: on an iOS simulator it writes the pasteboard from inside the device and does not depend on `simctl pbcopy`. A tvOS simulator has no pasteboard that `agent-device` can write from inside the device, so `clipboard write` on tvOS still uses `simctl pbcopy` and is subject to this problem.

## iOS: system prompts that ask for typed text accept no automated input

iOS shows some prompts outside the app under test: an Apple ID password field, a Screen Time passcode, a device passcode request. `fill` and `type` act inside the app under test, so they cannot enter text into these prompts, and no command enters text there. A prompt that only asks to continue or to cancel is answerable. A prompt that waits for typed text needs a person at the device.

**Workarounds:**

* **Avoid the prompt** with the `settings` channel: `settings permission grant <permission>` pre-grants a permission before the flow, and `settings faceid match` passes a biometric check without the passcode prompt. `settings` on iOS is simulator-only.
* **Answer without typing** with the `alert` channel: `alert accept` and `alert dismiss` press a recognized button, and `alert get` reads the labels of a prompt with unrecognized wording.

## iOS device: `alert` matches English labels only

On an iOS simulator, the runner also recognizes the device’s preferred-language wording of the alert labels it knows. A physical iOS device has no such translation step, and tvOS and visionOS devices are the same: `alert accept` and `alert dismiss` match the English labels only. When the device runs in another language, the prompt’s buttons carry localized labels, so `alert` answers `ALERT_BUTTON_NOT_FOUND` and taps nothing.

**Workaround:** read the labels with `alert get`, then capture the prompt with `snapshot -i` and `press @ref` on the visible button.

## Android: non-ASCII text on real devices needs `--test-ime`

`adb shell input text` cannot type non-ASCII text (for example Chinese characters or emoji) on any Android system image. `agent-device` installs its own headless test IME (`android-ime-helper`) to type that text. The test IME also keeps the on-screen system keyboard out of snapshots.

* **Emulators**: the test IME turns on automatically on `open`. Non-ASCII `fill` and `type` work without setup.
* **Real devices**: pass `--test-ime` to `open` to opt in. It is off by default on real hardware because a stuck helper IME leaves the real keyboard unavailable until restored. `agent-device` restores the previous IME when the session closes, and on daemon startup if a previous session crashed. If the keyboard still looks stuck, `agent-device doctor` flags it and prints the exact `adb shell ime set <id>` command that restores it.
* **`test` and `replay`**: pass `--test-ime` or `--no-test-ime` to the flow command, or set `testIme` in config. The setting applies to every session the flow run opens. Use this when a Maestro `eraseText` or non-ASCII `fill` step runs in a session the flow owns.

If a stale input session drops a `fill` commit, `agent-device` rebinds the helper and retries once. If it cannot confirm the rebind, text entry stops until it can. If keyboard restoration cannot read its recovery record, `close` reports a failure and keeps the record so startup recovery can retry.

With the test IME, `type` and `fill` fail if the helper does not acknowledge the command; `type` also fails if no editor is focused. For an older helper, reinstall a current version and reopen the session.

If the helper cannot be installed (locked-down managed devices, some cloud providers), text entry falls back to ASCII-only `adb shell input text`, and non-ASCII `fill` and `type` report that they cannot enter the text.

## Android: first helper install can wait on an OEM install dialog

Some OEM builds make the first install of a package go through the system package installer, and `adb install` waits until someone confirms it on the device screen. This applies to both `agent-device` helper APKs (the snapshot helper and the test IME), once per package. On ColorOS (reported on an OPPO Find N6), the first install needs two taps: confirm the install, then dismiss the completion screen. Later installs of the same package are silent.

On such a device, an unattended first Android snapshot times out with a helper install failure. Its hint tells you to check the device screen for a pending install confirmation. Confirm the prompts on the device and retry. If no dialog is showing, restart the ADB server as the hint says.

## Android: WSL needs Linux platform-tools

Under WSL, the Windows `adb.exe` (for example from an `ANDROID_HOME` under `/mnt/c`) answers `adb version` but treats every host path as a Windows path, so recordings, pulls, and installs fail.

Install Linux Android platform-tools inside WSL, put them first on `PATH`, and point `ANDROID_HOME` at a Linux SDK. `agent-device doctor` fails the toolchain check with reason `android_adb_windows_binary_on_posix_host` when `adb` reports a Windows install path or reports that it is running on Windows. The same check catches a Windows `adb.exe` reached from macOS or Linux through WSL interop or Wine.

## Android: no clipboard access over adb on Android 16

On Android 16 (API 36), `adb shell cmd clipboard` exits with status **0** but never touches the clipboard; it prints `No shell command implementation.` on stderr. AOSP’s clipboard service has no shell command implementation (not at `android13-release` through `android16-release`, nor on AOSP `main`), and physical devices ship the same service.

`agent-device` checks each device once and refuses instead of reporting a false success:

* `capabilities` omits `clipboard` on such a device.
* `clipboard read` and `clipboard write` fail with `UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION` and a hint naming the missing shell command and the substitute, instead of returning `text: ""` or “Clipboard updated”.

**Workaround:** verify a copy flow from the app side. Trigger the app’s copy action, paste into a focused text field, and read that field back with `snapshot`. This proves the app’s own clipboard write, which an adb-side read never could.

On a build that does implement `cmd clipboard`, Android 10+ still restricts clipboard reads to the app with input focus or the current input method service, and adb is neither. An adb-side read can therefore come back blank. `agent-device` reports the empty clipboard it received rather than guessing at a denial. If you hit this on such a build, file an issue with the output of `adb shell cmd clipboard get text; echo rc=$?`.

## HarmonyOS: no clipboard access over HDC

HarmonyOS HDC exposes no public clipboard interface. `agent-device` can therefore neither read nor write the HarmonyOS clipboard:

* `capabilities` does not list `clipboard` on a HarmonyOS device.
* `clipboard read` and `clipboard write` fail with `UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION`.

A copy-then-paste check on HarmonyOS therefore fails silently. The long-press paste flow still runs: the tap on **Paste** lands, and the field receives whatever the device clipboard already holds. Because `agent-device` cannot set that content, the paste can insert text that an earlier manual copy left on the device. The flow reports success, and you see the mismatch only when you read the field back.

**Workaround:** put the text into the field with `fill` or `type`. Both enter text through ArkUI `uitest` and need no clipboard. To verify the app’s own copy or paste UX, operate the device by hand, then read the field back with `snapshot`.

## HarmonyOS: Web and custom-drawn content can miss the accessibility tree

`snapshot` on HarmonyOS reads the ArkUI accessibility tree through `uitest`. Content that publishes no accessibility nodes has no entries in that tree: a Web component’s page, and custom-drawn surfaces such as a Canvas or a game view. When such content dominates the screen, the capture comes back sparse, and a sparse capture has no usable `@refs`.

**Workaround:** capture the screen with `screenshot`, read the image, and tap by coordinates (`click 120 340`). After a navigation, run `snapshot -i` again before you use refs.

# Limrun

> Drive Limrun iOS simulators and Android emulators with agent-device.

Use Limrun to run agent-device on remote iOS simulators and Android emulators. You need a Limrun API key, or the URL and token of an instance someone else created. Limrun does not use local or physical-device selectors such as `--udid`, `--serial`, or `--device`.

## Set credentials and connect

Export your Limrun API key, for example from CI secrets. Set `LIMRUN_REGION` to pick a region.

```bash
export LIMRUN_API_KEY=...
export AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION=checkout-android
agent-device connect limrun --platform android
```

`--platform android` or `--platform ios` selects the instance type. `connect` checks the credentials for that platform without creating an instance. Set `AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION` to a name for your agent or CI job. Every command on a Limrun connection needs that session name, either through this variable, `--session`, or your config.

Requests agent-device makes with your API key, including instance creation, start their `User-Agent` with `agent-device-cli/<version>` so Limrun can attribute them to agent-device for revenue sharing.

## Create and delete an instance

Use `boot` to allocate an instance explicitly before installing your app. This step is optional: `install` also allocates an instance when needed. If this connection already has an instance, `boot` reuses it.

`devices` lists only this connection’s instance, not the simulators or devices on your machine. Like `install`, the CLI allocates an instance first when the connection has none. An SDK call without a lease fails with `DEVICE_NOT_FOUND` and `details.reason: 'provider_instance_unallocated'`.

```bash
agent-device boot
agent-device shutdown
agent-device boot
```

`shutdown` deletes an instance that agent-device created, including its apps and data. The next `boot` creates a fresh instance. Limrun has no stopped instance to resume. If a session is open, use `close --shutdown` to end it and delete its instance. `shutdown` on a connection without an instance creates nothing and fails with `DEVICE_NOT_FOUND` and `details.reason: 'provider_instance_unallocated'`.

For an [existing instance](#drive-an-existing-instance), `boot` attaches and `shutdown` releases the attachment. The instance stays running, and its owner deletes it. `close --shutdown` also releases an attachment or lease allocated with `retainOnClose: true`.

## Drive an existing instance

An agent in a sandbox can drive an instance that someone else created, such as the instance behind a live preview, without your organization’s API key. Create the instance where the API key lives, then give the sandbox that instance’s URL and token from its `status`:

| Platform | Environment variables                                                                                                                                  |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| iOS      | `LIM_IOS_INSTANCE_URL` (`status.apiUrl`), `LIM_IOS_INSTANCE_TOKEN` (`status.token`)                                                                    |
| Android  | `LIM_ANDROID_INSTANCE_URL` (`status.apiUrl`), `LIM_ANDROID_INSTANCE_TOKEN` (`status.token`), `LIM_ANDROID_INSTANCE_ADB_URL` (`status.adbWebSocketUrl`) |

The `lim` CLI reads the same variables, so one set works for both tools. Set all of a platform’s variables or none. With a partial set, `connect` fails, and the daemon registers without Limrun, lists it as `failed` in `agent-device daemon status`, and records `provider_plugin_failed` in `daemon.log`.

```bash
export LIM_IOS_INSTANCE_URL=...
export LIM_IOS_INSTANCE_TOKEN=...
export AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION=preview-ios


agent-device connect limrun --platform ios
agent-device open com.example.app
agent-device snapshot -i
agent-device disconnect
```

`connect` checks the instance credentials. agent-device never creates or deletes that instance: `disconnect` leaves it running, and its owner deletes it. When a platform’s instance variables are set, they take precedence over `LIMRUN_API_KEY` for that platform.

On an attached Android instance, agent-device does not replace an existing port reverse mapping. If the owner already maps a device port, such as `tcp:8081` for their Metro server, a reverse to that port fails and the owner’s mapping stays in place. The error has `details.reason: 'android_port_reverse_rebind_refused'` when `adb reverse --list` shows the mapping; otherwise it is a plain ADB failure.

If your shell’s account variables, or its instance variables for the platform you lease, differ from the ones the daemon started with, the first `install` or `open` refuses before it creates or attaches to an instance. See [Change credentials while the daemon runs](/docs/device-clouds#change-credentials-while-the-daemon-runs).

`install` and `reinstall` sync local app files directly to the instance. An attached iOS instance needs its URL and token. An attached Android instance also needs `LIM_ANDROID_INSTANCE_ADB_URL` to connect the provider; the app upload itself uses HTTP. `apps` before the first `open` needs `LIMRUN_API_KEY` to list stored assets. After `open`, `apps` lists the apps installed on the instance without the key. From the Node.js runtime, `getDeviceSession(device).installRemoteApp(url)` installs from a signed asset URL without the API key.

## Keep idle sessions alive

Limrun ends an instance after its inactivity timeout, which an idle session can reach while a model thinks between steps. Set `LIMRUN_KEEP_ALIVE=1` (or `true`) to ping the instance every 30 seconds while a session is open. Keep-alive is off by default. In the Node.js runtime, pass `keepAlive: true`.

Two timers can end an idle Limrun session.

* The session lease. Each command that uses the lease renews it for five minutes. After five minutes without such a command the lease expires, and the daemon ends the session. The next command that uses the lease allocates a new lease, and the app you opened is not restored.
* The Limrun instance. An instance that agent-device creates ends after five minutes without activity, the same window as the lease. An instance you attach to keeps the inactivity timeout it was created with. When a created instance ends, the next command reports why it ended. Run `install` again to start a new instance and reinstall the app, then run `open`. For an attached instance, replace its connection details before you open again. agent-device reports an attached instance as ended only after its connection is closed for good. If the instance ends while the connection is still reconnecting, the lease ends when its five-minute window expires.

`LIMRUN_KEEP_ALIVE` keeps the instance running past five minutes. It does not renew the lease.

## Run a session from the CLI

A new Limrun instance does not contain your app. Run `install <package-or-bundle-id> <app-path-or-url>` before `open`. `install` allocates the instance when needed, so you do not need to run `devices` first.

```bash
export LIMRUN_API_KEY=...
export AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION=checkout-android


agent-device connect limrun --platform android
agent-device install com.example.app ./app.apk
agent-device open com.example.app --relaunch
agent-device snapshot -i
agent-device click 'label="Continue"'
agent-device close
agent-device disconnect
```

For a new iOS simulator, install a simulator build of your app:

```bash
export LIMRUN_API_KEY=...
export AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION=checkout-ios


agent-device connect limrun --platform ios
agent-device install com.example.app ./MyApp.app
agent-device open com.example.app
agent-device snapshot -i
agent-device screenshot ./screen.png
agent-device record start ./session.mp4
agent-device click 'label="Continue"'
agent-device record stop
agent-device close
agent-device disconnect
```

Use a selector from your app’s snapshot in place of `Continue`.

On Android, agent-device connects to Limrun over an ADB tunnel. Snapshots use the Android snapshot helper, local installs use HTTP delta sync, and port reverse runs over ADB, including the usual reverse setup for a local Metro server.

## Use an iOS simulator

Use the same snapshot, selector, text-entry, gesture, navigation, clipboard, and alert commands as on a local iOS simulator. Limrun iOS uses the agent-device XCTest runner. The runner reads snapshots with the same accessibility reader as a local iOS simulator, so snapshot output, selectors, and refs match local runs. When that reader cannot serve the screen, for example while a system sign-in sheet is open, the snapshot uses XCTest instead and says so in a warning. `fill` replaces text and `type` appends it; both support `--delay-ms`.

Use a stable agent-device release. It downloads and starts the matching runner automatically. You do not need local Xcode or any runner network configuration. Stop Appium or other XCTest sessions on the simulator before you start, because only one XCTest run can use it at a time. Limrun limits each XCTest run to one hour; close and reopen your session when it reaches that limit.

If startup fails with `limrun_xctest_slot_occupied`, stop the agent-device or Appium session that owns the simulator and wait for its XCTest run to end. If that client has exited and the slot remains occupied, recreate the Limrun instance. If a snapshot fails with `limrun_runner_snapshot_unavailable`, close and reopen your agent-device session. Recreate the instance if captures still fail. Do not reuse snapshot references after a failed capture.

Open your app before taking a snapshot. Snapshots target the app you opened in that session. In the SDK, you can also pass `appBundleId` to the snapshot call. A snapshot without a target app fails.

`install` leaves your app stopped. Use `open` to launch it. To change launch arguments on an app that is already running, use `open --relaunch --launch-args`. Screenshots download as lossless PNG files, and recording downloads the finished MP4 when you stop it. Push notifications use the same command and payload format as local simulators.

If you use a nightly or unpublished agent-device build, obtain a matching packaged iOS runner from the build’s maintainer. Set `AGENT_DEVICE_LIMRUN_IOS_RUNNER_APP` to the extracted `.app` path before starting agent-device. The runner must be built with Xcode 27, because Limrun runs XCTest with Xcode 27. agent-device refuses a runner built with an older Xcode. If the daemon is already running, stop it with `agent-device daemon stop` using the same `--state-dir`, then reconnect.

## Connect an iOS app to Metro

An installed Expo dev client can open with the same automatic launch URL discovery as a local simulator when its `exp+` scheme has one installed owner and Metro runtime information is available. An explicit launch URL takes precedence. If agent-device cannot verify which app owns a custom URL scheme, it leaves the launch confirmation for you to inspect and answer with the alert commands.

For a local Metro server, connect with `--provider-network-logs` and include `localhost:8081`, or your Metro port, in `--provider-network-hosts`. While the session is open, the app can reach that port on the machine running agent-device. See [Capture session network traffic](#capture-session-network-traffic) for the network changes this option makes. Otherwise, use a publicly reachable HTTPS Metro endpoint. `port reverse` is Android-only.

## Read Android performance data

On an open Android session, use the same commands as on a local emulator:

```bash
agent-device perf frames --json
agent-device perf memory sample --json
agent-device perf memory snapshot --kind android-hprof --out ./heap.hprof
```

Frame statistics and memory samples describe the running app. A heap snapshot downloads an HPROF file to your machine; the app must permit heap dumps. Reading frame statistics resets the app’s frame counters, as it does locally. Native Simpleperf and Perfetto captures remain unavailable through the Limrun provider.

Android `get text` also uses the shared live text reader when the selected element supports it.

## Read iOS app logs

After opening your app, use `logs start` to collect its stdout, stderr, and matching simulator logs. Use `open <app> --launch-console <path>` to capture its initial launch output. Runner logs contain the test results Limrun provides, but native XCTest stdout is unavailable.

Remote simulator logs do not include sender or process image paths. Filters that rely only on those fields cannot match remotely.

## Change simulator settings

On iOS, `settings` supports `appearance`, `permission`, `location`, `wifi`, `airplane`, `faceid`, `touchid`, `text-size`, and `clear-app-state`, with the same arguments as a local simulator. You can also read the current text size.

Wi-Fi and airplane settings change the status-bar appearance; they do not disconnect the simulator. `clear-app-state` stops your app and removes its data. Use `open` when you are ready to launch it again. `reset-keychain` and `mobile-data` are unavailable on Limrun iOS. On Android, `settings mobile-data on|off` works as on a local device. Fold commands are unavailable on Limrun.

To drive Limrun only through MCP, see [Use a provider only through MCP](/docs/device-clouds#use-a-provider-only-through-mcp). For Limrun, `artifacts` lists the network capture file only when you connect with `--provider-network-logs`; otherwise there are no provider artifacts to fetch.

## Capture session network traffic

Use `--provider-network-logs` when you debug an app’s network requests on a remote Limrun device. The device’s traffic is captured while the session runs. `agent-device artifacts` and `close` write it as a HAR 1.2 file and print its path.

Before you turn it on, know what the capture changes:

* Captured traffic leaves through the machine that runs agent-device, not the device’s own network. Servers see that machine’s public IP. On CI, the traffic leaves from the CI runner.
* The HAR holds raw requests and responses, including headers, cookies, tokens, and bodies. Treat it as a secret. Keep it out of logs, bug reports, and build artifacts that others can read.
* Some hosts can’t be captured: certificate-pinned hosts refuse the connection, apps that resolve names over DNS-over-HTTPS bypass the capture, and HTTPS hosts that don’t support HTTP/2 fail to connect.
* Each body is cut to 64 KiB, and the HAR keeps the latest 500 requests.

Pass your app’s API hosts with `--provider-network-hosts`, then open the app after you connect:

```bash
export AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION=checkout-ios
agent-device connect limrun --platform ios --provider-network-logs \
  --provider-network-hosts "api.example.com,*.cdn.example.com,localhost:8081"
agent-device open com.example.app
agent-device artifacts      # writes the HAR and prints its path
jq -r '.log.entries[] | "\(.response.status) \(.request.method) \(.request.url)"' <har-path>
agent-device close          # writes the HAR again and prints its path
agent-device disconnect
```

`--provider-network-hosts` takes exact hosts, wildcards such as `*.example.com`, and `localhost:<port>` routes. Keep `localhost:8081`, or your Metro port, in the list when the app loads its bundle from a local Metro server. Without `--provider-network-hosts`, the capture covers every `.com`, `.org`, `.app`, `.net`, `.io`, and `.dev` host plus `localhost:8081`. System traffic then fills most of the file.

The file is `<state-dir>/network-har/<lease-id>.har`, and only your user can read it. It stays until you delete it. If the capture can’t start, for example because a `--provider-network-hosts` entry is not a valid host, `artifacts` reports the network artifact as `unavailable` with the reason.

A request that can’t reach its host appears in the HAR with status `0`. When the capture has failures, `artifacts` and `close` print a summary after the HAR path:

```text
Network capture failures: 2; last request-failed api.example.com:443; last dial failure dns_not_found
```

The count includes these kinds: `request-failed` (the host didn’t resolve, refused, timed out, or failed TLS), `inspection-error` (usually a certificate-pinned host), and `inspection-gap` and `inspection-stream-error` (the HAR misses requests). `last dial failure` is Limrun’s reason for the most recent failed connection. The HAR keeps the latest 500 requests, with each body cut to 64 KiB, so a capture can hold tens of MB in the daemon. When older requests left the HAR, the summary says how many, and the count doesn’t include them. `artifacts --json` returns the same values in `data.cloudArtifacts[0].metadata.failures`.

Now and then, a request skips the capture: it is missing from the HAR and from the failure count. If a request you expect is missing, repeat it. If the HAR stays empty while the app makes requests, run `close` and `disconnect`, then connect again.

## Embed the Node.js runtime

A Node.js bridge, such as agent-device-cloud, can embed agent-device’s Limrun runtime:

```ts
import { LimrunRuntime } from 'agent-device/limrun';


const apiKey = process.env.LIMRUN_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error('LIMRUN_API_KEY is required');


const runtime = new LimrunRuntime({
  apiKey,
  region: process.env.LIMRUN_REGION,
});
```

To drive existing instances, pass `instances: { ios: { apiUrl, token } }` (Android also takes `adbUrl`), with or without `apiKey`. The runtime never creates or deletes instances for a platform listed there.

A provider that reaches a harness-owned instance through the Node.js client allocates a Limrun lease in `acquire` and releases that same lease in `release`. Put the returned `lease.leaseId` on the client scope, and pass that same id to `leases.release`. Start the daemon with the instance URL and token (`LIM_IOS_INSTANCE_URL` and `LIM_IOS_INSTANCE_TOKEN`). `leases.allocate` attaches to that instance. `leases.release` returns `{ released, provider }`. Neither call creates or deletes the instance. Allocate with `retainOnClose: true` because the provider releases the lease itself: without it, a session `close` before `release` ends the lease and `leases.release` returns `released: false`. A retained lease still expires after its `ttlMs`, so keep heartbeating it between sessions. On iOS, a retained lease can reuse a healthy runner between sessions in the same daemon. Releasing the lease or stopping the daemon stops the runner. A new daemon cannot adopt it.

```ts
import { createAgentDeviceClient } from 'agent-device';


const scope = {
  tenant: 'limrun',
  runId: process.env.GITHUB_RUN_ID ?? 'local-run',
  leaseBackend: 'ios-instance',
  leaseProvider: 'limrun',
} as const;


const provider = {
  acquire: async (req: { slot: string }) => {
    const lease = await createAgentDeviceClient({ session: `lease-${req.slot}` }).leases.allocate({
      ...scope,
      platform: 'ios',
      retainOnClose: true,
    });
    return {
      id: lease.leaseId,
      client: { ...scope, leaseId: lease.leaseId, sessionIsolation: 'tenant' as const },
    };
  },
  release: async (lease: { id: string }) => {
    await createAgentDeviceClient({}).leases.release({ ...scope, leaseId: lease.id });
  },
};
```

After allocating a lease, call `runtime.getDeviceSession(device)` to get the allocated device’s capabilities: app inventory, foreground state where Limrun exposes it, key input, bounded log reads, recording, remote asset installation, and the interactor. On Android it also exposes agent-device’s `AndroidAdbProvider` for helpers and reversible port forwarding. On iOS it exposes a typed `simctl` execution handle so your bridge can own runner lifecycle and launch policy. The runtime does not expose raw Limrun clients.

## Record the screen

Use `record start video.mp4` and `record stop` in an open session. The recording runs on Limrun, and `record stop` downloads the finished MP4. Each agent-device recording has its own Limrun recording ID, so stopping it leaves other recordings on that instance running. Concurrent recordings must use compatible encoder settings, including the same quality.

`--quality medium|high` is supported. `--fps`, `--hide-touches`, and recording recovery after a daemon restart are not supported. Every recording scope captures the whole device screen.

## Get artifacts and troubleshoot

For Limrun, `agent-device artifacts` lists only the `--provider-network-logs` HAR file. If a page hangs while the capture runs, read the failure summary that `artifacts` prints; see [Capture session network traffic](#capture-session-network-traffic). If `connect` fails, check `LIMRUN_API_KEY` and the optional `LIMRUN_REGION`. For an existing instance, check its URL and token variables, and that the instance is still running.

# Rewrite old gesture commands

`swipe`, `gesture fling`, and `gesture swipe` don’t take a duration, and `gesture rotate` doesn’t take a velocity. A command, script, or client call that passes one fails with an `INVALID_ARGS` error that names its replacement; nothing is silently reinterpreted.

Find your surface below — CLI, Node.js, MCP, or saved `.ad` recordings — and apply its rewrite.

## Throws and drags

Gesture commands separate a *throw* from a *deliberate drag*:

* `swipe` and `gesture fling` are quick, fixed-duration directional throws. They do not take a duration; a timed movement is a drag, which is `gesture pan`.
* `gesture pan` is the deliberate timed translation. It keeps `durationMs`.
* `gesture rotate` derives its pacing from the requested `degrees`.

`durationMs` remains on `gesture pan` and `gesture transform`.

## CLI

| Old form                                            | Use instead                              |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `swipe x1 y1 x2 y2 durationMs`                      | `gesture pan x1 y1 dx dy durationMs`     |
| `gesture fling <direction> x y distance durationMs` | `gesture fling <direction> x y distance` |
| `gesture swipe <preset> durationMs`                 | `gesture swipe <preset>`                 |
| `gesture rotate degrees x y velocity`               | `gesture rotate degrees x y`             |

`gesture pan` takes an origin plus a **delta**, where `swipe` took two absolute points, so `dx = x2 - x1` and `dy = y2 - y1`:

```bash
# before
agent-device swipe 197 650 197 300 300
# after — same motion, same 300ms
agent-device gesture pan 197 650 0 -350 300
```

If you wanted a throw and the duration did not matter, drop the duration instead. The result is a 100ms fling, which travels further on a scrollable list than a 300ms drag over the same distance:

```bash
agent-device swipe 197 650 197 300
```

The error message includes both rewrites with your coordinates filled in:

```plaintext
swipe accepts 4 arguments: x1 y1 x2 y2. The trailing durationMs positional was removed:
use "gesture pan 197 650 0 -350 300" for the same timed drag, or "swipe 197 650 197 300"
for a default-duration swipe.
```

## Node.js

`interactions.swipe`, `interactions.fling`, and `interactions.swipeGesture` don’t accept `durationMs`; `interactions.rotateGesture` doesn’t accept `velocity`. Passing them is a type error at compile time and an `INVALID_ARGS` rejection at runtime. The client rejects the call before it reaches the daemon, so plain JavaScript and stale compiled builds get the error rather than a silently retimed gesture.

```ts
// before
await device.interactions.swipe({
  from: { x: 197, y: 650 },
  to: { x: 197, y: 300 },
  durationMs: 300,
});


// after — same motion, same 300ms
await device.interactions.pan({ x: 197, y: 650, dx: 0, dy: -350, durationMs: 300 });


// after — a default-duration throw
await device.interactions.swipe({ from: { x: 197, y: 650 }, to: { x: 197, y: 300 } });
```

`interactions.pan` and `interactions.transformGesture` keep `durationMs`.

## MCP

The `swipe`, `gesture` (`fling`, `swipe` kinds), and `gesture rotate` tool schemas don’t advertise `durationMs` or `velocity`, so an agent reading the schema will not produce the old form. An agent that sends one anyway — from a cached schema or a memorized example — gets an `INVALID_ARGS` rejection that names the rejected key and the command to use instead, for example `gesture fling does not accept durationMs; use gesture pan for timed movement`. Unlike the CLI and `.ad` errors, the MCP error names the replacement command without a filled-in rewrite.

You do not need to change your MCP server configuration.

## Saved `.ad` recordings

`.ad` scripts keep their positional syntax, which matches the CLI (see [Positional `.ad` syntax](#positional-ad-syntax) below). Remove only the duration or velocity argument.

A script that still carries one fails **when it is parsed**, before the replay executes any device action, and the error names the line:

```plaintext
Error (INVALID_ARGS): swipe accepts 4 arguments: x1 y1 x2 y2 (line 6). The trailing durationMs
positional was removed: use "gesture pan 197 650 0 -350 300" for the same timed drag, or
"swipe 197 650 197 300" for a default-duration swipe.
```

Apply the same rewrites as the CLI table above. Flags are unaffected: `--count`, `--pause-ms`, and `--pattern` stay on `swipe`, and `--pointer-count` stays on `gesture pan`.

```plaintext
# before
swipe 206 650 206 300 300 --count 2 --pause-ms 200 --pattern one-way
# after
swipe 206 650 206 300 --count 2 --pause-ms 200 --pattern one-way
```

A duration held in a variable (`swipe 197 650 197 300 ${DURATION}`) is reported the same way: the check counts arguments, so it does not need the value.

**Running your scripts is the definitive check.** Every old form is rejected when the script is parsed, before the replay runs any device action, so `agent-device test <glob>` or `agent-device replay <file>.ad` finds and names every stale line. To locate them in bulk without a device, use the patterns below. They split tokens on any whitespace (space or tab) and match a bare or double-quoted number or `${VAR}` in each numeric slot, so `swipe\t…\t"300"` is flagged like `swipe … 300`. They miss rarer spellings, such as a quoted command word or backslash escapes inside a quoted token, so treat a clean grep as a first pass and the run as the proof.

```bash
# a numeric slot: bare/quoted number (optionally signed) or ${VAR}. Requiring a
# digit keeps a following flag like --count from being read as the extra slot.
num='("-?[0-9][0-9.]*"|"\$\{[^}]*\}"|-?[0-9][0-9.]*|\$\{[^}]*\})'
# swipe x1 y1 x2 y2 durationMs
grep -rnE "\\bswipe([[:space:]]+$num){5}" --include='*.ad' .
# gesture fling <direction> x y distance durationMs
grep -rnE "\\bgesture[[:space:]]+fling[[:space:]]+\"?[a-z]+\"?([[:space:]]+$num){4}" --include='*.ad' .
# gesture swipe <preset> durationMs
grep -rnE "\\bgesture[[:space:]]+swipe[[:space:]]+\"?[a-z-]+\"?[[:space:]]+$num" --include='*.ad' .
# gesture rotate degrees x y velocity
grep -rnE "\\bgesture[[:space:]]+rotate([[:space:]]+$num){4}" --include='*.ad' .
```

Instead of editing by hand, you can re-record: the recorder writes the current form, so a fresh `open --save-script` → interact → `close` run produces a script in the current form. Recording starts at `open`, so pass `--save-script` there; `close --save-script` on a session opened without it is rejected.

### Maestro flows

Maestro `swipe` with a `duration` is **not** affected, and Maestro flows need no changes. `agent-device` runs a timed Maestro swipe as `gesture pan` and keeps Maestro’s fast-swipe-then-hold timing.

`replay export` writes an explicit `duration: 100`, the fling duration, so an exported flow runs at the speed the `.ad` script ran instead of Maestro’s 400ms default.

## Positional `.ad` syntax

Positional gesture arguments in `.ad` are the file format itself, not a compatibility shim. `.ad` is a line-based script format that uses the CLI’s syntax. Node.js and MCP send structured input; the CLI and `.ad` files use positional arguments. Keeping `.ad` positional keeps recordings readable and searchable with grep.

See [ADR 0013](https://github.com/callstack/agent-device/blob/main/docs/adr/0013-unified-gesture-plans.md) for the gesture normalization and planning model this rests on.

# Provider plugins

Provider plugins add device providers that agent-device does not bundle, such as [TestMu AI](/docs/testmu), [LG webOS](/docs/webos), and [Samsung Tizen](/docs/tizen). Installing one requires npm on your host:

```bash
agent-device plugins add @example/agent-device-provider
agent-device plugins list --json
agent-device plugins update @example/agent-device-provider
agent-device plugins remove @example/agent-device-provider
```

`agent-device help connect` and `agent-device help remote` identify known optional providers as `plugin, install separately` and show their installation commands, even before you install them. For example, TestMu AI requires `agent-device plugins add @agent-device/testmu`.

If you run `agent-device connect testmu` without its plugin, the error gives that installation command and tells you to retry your original command. With `--json`, the error has `details.reason: plugin-not-installed`, `details.package`, and `details.installCommand`. If the plugin is selected but unavailable, the reason is `plugin-unavailable`; run `agent-device plugins list --json` to inspect it, then fix its configuration or update the package.

Use a full npm package name, optionally with `@version` or `@tag`. `update` keeps valid version constraints and options, including when it repairs a damaged selection. To change a constraint, run `add <package>@<version-or-tag>`; to remove it, run `add <package>` without a suffix.

Each installation lives in an npm project with a lockfile under `AGENT_DEVICE_HOME` (default `~/.agent-device`), and that directory’s `config.json` records the selection. Plugin commands leave other settings in `config.json` unchanged. Project config and `--config` cannot select plugins. This home is independent of `--state-dir` and `AGENT_DEVICE_STATE_DIR`.

Install only packages you trust: plugin factories run with the daemon’s host permissions and environment. Installs skip lifecycle scripts, so packages must contain ready-to-run JavaScript and assets.

A failed install keeps the previous selection. A running daemon keeps the plugin set and files it started with, including removed installations. To apply changes, close sessions and run `agent-device daemon stop` with the matching `--state-dir`; the next device command uses the new set. Use separate state directories for different plugin homes.

## See which providers are registered

`agent-device daemon status` lists every provider the running daemon registered: the bundled ones (BrowserStack, AWS Device Farm, and Limrun when it is configured), then installed plugins. With `--json`, each entry has:

```json
{
  "provider": "testmu",
  "source": "store",
  "package": "@agent-device/testmu",
  "version": "0.21.29",
  "state": "active",
  "credentials": { "variables": ["LT_USERNAME", "LT_ACCESS_KEY"], "byBackend": {} }
}
```

`source` is `builtin` or `store`; `embedder` is the third slot, reserved for plugins an embedding host passes itself (#3757). A plugin that cannot register has `state: "failed"` and an `error` with `code`, `message`, and a `reason` such as `invalid_plugin`, `incompatible_plugin`, or `duplicate_provider`. The daemon starts without it and keeps every other provider. Fix or remove the package, then stop the daemon so the next command starts a new one.

When a daemon’s `daemon.json` cannot be used, `daemon status` says so instead of reporting a stopped daemon: `unreadable` means the file exists but could not be read, and `invalid` means it was read but is not a daemon record. A missing or stale record means `stopped`; an unreadable or invalid file never does.

When the daemon stops, it closes every plugin once: each runtime shuts down, then its `dispose` runs. A step that fails is logged as `provider_plugin_cleanup_failed` with the provider and step, and the other plugins still close.

`plugins list --json` works without a daemon. It lists your installed plugins with their provider and whether their factory loads and validates; whether `setup` succeeds shows only in a running daemon’s inventory. When a daemon is running for the same `--state-dir`, it also reports that daemon’s inventory under `daemon`.

When two plugins claim the same provider, the first one wins: bundled providers, then installed plugins in package-name order, then, once #3757 lets an embedding host pass plugins, those. The others are `failed` with `duplicate_provider`. The first claim holds even when that plugin then fails to set up, so a later plugin for the same provider doesn’t take over. `cloud` and `proxy` are reserved and can’t be claimed.

A lease that names a provider this daemon has no runtime for refuses with `UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION` and reason `provider-not-registered`, before any lease is recorded. The error lists the registered providers and, as `failedPlugins`, any plugin that failed to register for that provider (or failed before its provider was known); restart the daemon with the provider’s plugin installed. Leases with no provider, `proxy`, and `cloud` need no provider runtime.

## Create a plugin

The interface is experimental. A plugin package exports a factory at `./agent-device`. Use `agent-device` as a development dependency; plugins import only types from it.

```json
{
  "name": "@example/agent-device-provider",
  "type": "module",
  "exports": {
    "./agent-device": { "import": "./dist/plugin.mjs" }
  }
}
```

```ts
import type { AgentDevicePluginFactory } from 'agent-device/plugins';


type ExampleOptions = { credentials?: { username: string; accessKey: string } };


const example: AgentDevicePluginFactory<ExampleOptions> = (options = {}) => ({
  apiVersion: 2,
  provider: 'example',
  credentials: {
    // Variables the daemon reads credentials from; none when the caller passes them as options.
    variables: options.credentials ? [] : ['EXAMPLE_USERNAME', 'EXAMPLE_ACCESS_KEY'],
  },
  setup: async (host) => ({ runtime, platformModule }),
});


export default example;
```

The factory is called with the package’s `options` from `config.json` (`plugins["<package>"].options`; leave `installation` unchanged). A JavaScript host that imports the package calls the same factory directly with its own options.

The host resolves the `./agent-device` export with import conditions. It falls back to the package’s root export only when that subpath does not exist. If the subpath exists but its import or `setup` throws, the plugin is reported as failed and the root export is not tried.

`setup(host)` receives `ProviderPluginHost`: `env`, `options`, `clientVersion`, and `createError` for host-recognized errors. Return one of:

* `{ runtime, platformModule, dispose? }` implementing the [provider runtime](https://github.com/callstack/agent-device/blob/main/packages/contracts/src/provider-device-runtime.ts) and [platform module](https://github.com/callstack/agent-device/blob/main/packages/contracts/src/platform-runtime-operations.ts) contracts. The runtime’s `provider` and the module owner’s `provider` must equal the plugin’s `provider`, and the module owner must declare `kind: 'provider-runtime'` and a nonempty `instance`.
* `{ webDriver, dispose? }` for an Appium or WebDriver service. `WebDriverPluginOptions` is available through the type-only `agent-device/plugins/webdriver` import. The host supplies the client version and creates the shared runtime. Provider callbacks prepare sessions, upload apps, and retrieve artifacts.

The host checks required runtime methods and owner metadata when it sets the plugin up; operation contracts are checked when used. `dispose` runs once after the runtime shuts down. A failing `setup` cleans up its own resources; the host shuts down a runtime it already received if validation then refuses it.

Keep the factory and `setup` fast, with no network I/O or device allocation; a stalled plugin delays daemon startup. Load platform mechanics through `platformModule.loadRuntime` and perform remote work in request-bound operations.

Incompatible contract changes require a new `apiVersion`. Plugins can’t replace bundled providers or register arbitrary commands.

### Credentials

List the environment variables the provider reads in `credentials.variables`. A local daemon keeps the values it started with; when the shell holds different ones, the first command that allocates a lease refuses with reason `provider-credentials-changed` until the daemon is stopped. The check treats a whitespace-only value as unset. If a lease reads fewer variables on one backend, narrow them with `credentials.byBackend`, for example `{ "android-instance": ["EXAMPLE_API_KEY"] }`. Credentials the caller passes as factory options are not in the environment, so list no variable for them.

### Connect

To support `agent-device connect example`, add a `connection` to the plugin:

```ts
connection: {
  capabilities: {
    leaseKind: 'direct-device-provider',
    requiresAppAttachment: false,
    requiresRemoteDaemon: false,
    supportsArtifacts: false,
    supportsDeferredAppSelection: true,
    supportsDirectPortReverse: false,
    usesCloudWebDriverLease: false,
    holdsCloudDevice: false,
  },
  resolve: async ({ flags, env, cwd, stateDir, host }) => ({ profile }),
  verify: async ({ flags, env, host }) => verification,
},
```

`resolve` validates provider flags and returns `{ profile, extraFlags? }`; `profile.leaseProvider` must match the plugin’s `provider`. The host supplies connection identity, session defaults, Metro settings, and persists the profile. `verify` returns the provider verification result. Both also receive `host`, the same `ProviderPluginHost` that `setup` gets, built from the `env` of that call. Both run without allocating a device or setting up a runtime. `agent-device` loads installed plugins’ factories, not their `setup`, to read these capabilities. Set the optional `holdsCloudDevice: true` when the provider leases a cloud-hosted device. Each command that uses the lease then requests a five-minute lease window, the same as a proxy or cloud WebDriver lease, not the 60-second daemon default. A daemon whose `AGENT_DEVICE_LEASE_MAX_TTL_MS` is below five minutes refuses that request with `INVALID_ARGS`.

### Package for installation

Bundle the plugin implementation and ship ready-to-run ESM: installation disables lifecycle scripts. Bundle shared helpers with the plugin; `AppError` carries a shared brand so the host preserves its code and details across package copies. Import types with `import type` to keep them out of the runtime dependency graph.

## Version 1 plugins

Packages that declare `agentDevicePlugin` with `apiVersion: 1` in `package.json` keep working. The host reads the manifest’s `provider`, `entry`, `connection`, and `credentialVariables` before running any plugin code, then calls the default export with `ProviderPluginHost` and registers the `{ runtime, platformModule }` or `{ webDriver, connection? }` it returns. Support for this form ends in a later release; move to the `./agent-device` factory.

```json
{"agentDevicePlugin": {"apiVersion": 1, "provider": "example", "entry": "./dist/plugin.mjs"}}
```

A package that exports `./agent-device` is loaded as a version 2 plugin even if it also keeps the manifest, so one package can serve both old and new hosts.

# Quick start

Open an app, read its UI, and interact with it from the command line.

Before you start, [install `agent-device`](/docs/installation) and the platform tools for your target: Xcode for iOS, the Android SDK and ADB for Android, or the HarmonyOS Command Line Tools for HarmonyOS. To set up Cursor, Codex, Claude Code, Windsurf, Cline, Goose, or another coding agent, see [AI agent setup](/docs/agent-setup). To give an agent the whole documentation as one text file, use [llms-full.txt](https://agent-device.dev/llms-full.txt).

Device automation follows this pattern:

```bash
# 1. Discover the installed app identifier when needed
agent-device apps --platform ios # or android or harmonyos


# 2. Open the app
agent-device open SampleApp --platform ios # or android or harmonyos


# 3. Snapshot to get element refs
agent-device snapshot -i
# Output:
# @e1 [heading] "Sample App"
# @e2 [button] "Settings"
# [off-screen below] 2 interactive items: "Privacy", "Battery"


# 4. Interact using refs
agent-device click @e2


# 5. Snapshot again before the next interaction; if a target only appears in an off-screen summary, scroll and snapshot again first
agent-device snapshot -i


# 6. Optional: see what changed since the last snapshot
agent-device diff snapshot
# or, from snapshot-focused help/examples:
agent-device snapshot --diff
```

React Native dev and debug builds often show warning or error overlays that can intercept taps or hide the real UI. Check for them after opening the app and after major transitions. If they aren’t what you’re testing, dismiss them and continue, and mention them in your summary.

If no device, simulator, or emulator is running, boot one:

```bash
agent-device boot --platform ios # or android
# Android emulator launch by AVD name (GUI mode):
agent-device boot --platform android --device Pixel_9_Pro_XL
# Android headless emulator boot (AVD name):
agent-device boot --platform android --device Pixel_9_Pro_XL --headless
# Shut down a simulator or emulator when finished:
agent-device shutdown --platform ios
agent-device shutdown --platform android --device Pixel_9_Pro_XL
```

## Common commands

```bash
agent-device apps --platform android    # Discover the exact package name when unsure
agent-device capabilities --platform android # List the commands this target supports
agent-device open SampleApp
agent-device snapshot -i                 # Get visible interactive elements with refs
agent-device diff snapshot               # Show what changed since the last snapshot
agent-device click @e2                   # Click by ref
agent-device fill @e3 "test@example.com" # Clear then type (Android verifies and retries once if needed)
agent-device press @e3
agent-device type " more" --delay-ms 80  # Append into the already focused field
agent-device get text @e1                # Get text content
agent-device screenshot page.png         # Save to a specific path
agent-device install com.example.app ./build/app.apk     # Install the app, keeping app data where supported
agent-device install-from-source https://example.com/builds/app.apk --platform android
agent-device reinstall com.example.app ./build/app.apk   # Uninstall, then install with fresh state
agent-device shutdown --platform android --device Pixel_9_Pro_XL
agent-device close
```

`install` and `reinstall` accept `.apk` and `.aab` on Android, `.app` and `.ipa` on iOS, and `.hap` on HarmonyOS. For `.aab` requirements, `.ipa` archives with several apps, and installing from a URL, see [App install](/docs/commands#app-install-in-place).

If `open` fails because no simulator, emulator, or device is booted, run `boot --platform ios|android` and retry. If `open` fails because the app ID is wrong or missing, run `apps` and retry with the package name or bundle ID it lists.

## Run several steps in one command

When an agent already knows a short sequence of actions, send them as one batch:

```bash
agent-device batch \
  --platform ios \
  --steps-file /tmp/batch-steps.json \
  --json
```

Example batch payload for a known chat flow:

```json
[
  { "command": "open", "input": { "app": "ChatApp", "platform": "android" } },
  { "command": "click", "input": { "selector": "label=\"Travel chat\"" } },
  {
    "command": "wait",
    "input": { "selector": "label=\"Message\"", "timeoutMs": 3000 }
  },
  {
    "command": "fill",
    "input": {
      "selector": "label=\"Message\"",
      "text": "Sent the update"
    }
  },
  { "command": "press", "input": { "selector": "label=\"Send\"" } }
]
```

See [Batching](/docs/batching) for the payload format, failure handling, and best practices.

## Find elements without refs

Use `find` to target elements by visible text, label, or role:

```bash
agent-device find "Sign In" click
agent-device find label "Email" fill "user@example.com"
agent-device find role button click
```

## Replay a flow

To record and replay deterministic scripts, see [Replay and E2E testing](/docs/replay-e2e).

## Scroll

Scroll to reach content outside the viewport:

```bash
agent-device scroll down 0.5            # Scroll down half screen
agent-device scroll up 0.3              # Scroll up 30%
agent-device scroll down --pixels 320   # Scroll down by a fixed distance
```

## Change device settings

```bash
agent-device settings wifi on
agent-device settings airplane on
agent-device settings appearance toggle
agent-device settings clear-app-state
agent-device settings location off
agent-device settings location set 37.3349 -122.009
agent-device settings permission grant camera
```

iOS `settings` commands work on simulators only. On macOS, only `settings appearance ...` and `settings permission <grant|reset> <accessibility|screen-recording|input-monitoring>` are supported.

## Get JSON output

Add `--json` to parse output in scripts:

```bash
agent-device snapshot --json
agent-device get text @e1 --json
```

The default snapshot text is a compact view meant for agents to plan and target actions. Use `--raw` or `--json` when you need the full provider tree.

# Remote proxy

> Run agent-device on a Mac with simulator or device access and control it from another machine through an HTTP tunnel.

Use `agent-device proxy` when the machine running your agent cannot access the iOS simulator, Android emulator, or physical device directly, but another Mac can. The proxy runs on the device host, fronts the local daemon over HTTP, and lets a remote `agent-device` client call it through cloudflared, ngrok, or another tunnel.

The proxy authenticates clients with a bearer token. You do not need `agent-device auth`.

## Start the proxy on the device host

On the Mac with simulator or device access, start a tunnel to the proxy’s local port and keep that terminal open:

```bash
cloudflared tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:4310
```

For ngrok, use `ngrok http 4310` instead.

Read the public HTTPS origin printed by the tunnel. In a second terminal, start the proxy with that origin, replacing `https://example.trycloudflare.com` with yours:

```bash
agent-device proxy --port 4310 --public-origin https://example.trycloudflare.com
```

**`--public-origin` is required when the tunnel terminates TLS**, so app uploads use HTTPS. Use the scheme, host and optional port, without the `/agent-device` path. If the tunnel URL changes, restart the proxy with the new origin.

The command prints the local proxy URL and a `daemon auth token`. Keep the token secret: anyone who has it can control the daemon behind the proxy.

By default the proxy binds `127.0.0.1`. Use `--host 0.0.0.0` only when you want the proxy reachable from the host network.

## Connect from the agent machine

On the machine running the agent, connect to the public tunnel URL with the `/agent-device` base path and the printed token. The connection profile stores only routing metadata, never the token, so export the token once and every command in the shell picks it up. Name the session the same way:

```bash
export AGENT_DEVICE_DAEMON_AUTH_TOKEN=<token>
export AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION=checkout-agent
agent-device connect proxy --daemon-base-url https://example.trycloudflare.com/agent-device
agent-device devices --platform ios
agent-device open MyApp --platform ios
agent-device snapshot --platform ios
agent-device close
agent-device disconnect
```

Every command on a proxy connection that takes a session must name it, with `AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION`, `--session <name>`, or a `session` in your config. The same applies to every device-cloud connection. A command that names none fails with `INVALID_ARGS` and `details.reason: "REMOTE_SESSION_REQUIRED"`, and sends nothing to the proxy. It never falls back to the connection that another agent on the same machine saved last. This includes `connect proxy` and `open --remote-config <file>` with a proxy profile. The client and run that the proxy leases under come from the session name, so two agents with different names never share a lease.

`--daemon-auth-token <token>` works instead of the environment variable, but it authenticates only the command you pass it to. Later commands need the token again through the environment variable, a `daemonAuthToken` entry in your remote config profile, or the flag on each command.

`connect proxy` stores the proxy profile and client identity. `open` leases the device for you, and the lease expires after five minutes without commands. A lease allocated directly over the RPC without `ttlMs` gets the daemon’s one-minute inactivity default instead. Either window starts when allocation completes, not when it was requested. `close` releases the active session and its device lease, unless the lease was allocated with `retainOnClose`; only `leases.release`, expiry, or daemon shutdown ends that one. The reply to any request that closed a session lists the leases it ended in `endedLeases`, as `{ leaseId, outcome: 'released' }`. This covers `close`, a `batch` with a close step, and a `replay` or `test` script that closes, as well as the session cleanup `test` runs after each script. A successful reply has the field in `data`, and a failed one has it in `error.details`. A gateway in front of the daemon reads the lease end from that reply. When the reply names the stored lease, the CLI forgets it, so the next `open` leases a device again. `disconnect` clears local connection state.

Without `--udid` or `--serial`, `open` does not pick the device on the agent machine: it sends `--platform`, `--target`, and `--device` with the lease request, the daemon behind the proxy picks a matching device, and later commands use the device the lease names. The device therefore does not need to exist before `open`, which lets a service in front of the daemon create or choose it at that point. While that lease is active, an `open` that names a different device is refused instead of running on the leased one; close the session first, or run `connect --force` to start over. An existing lease that names no device, such as one supplied through `leaseId`, is refused with reason `LEASE_SCOPE_MISMATCH` and left active.

`open` names each new lease with an id it makes (32 lowercase hex characters) and sends it with the allocation, so a host in front of the daemon knows the lease id before the daemon allocates. A direct `agent_device.lease.allocate` RPC can pass `leaseId` (16 to 128 hex characters) the same way; repeating the id of a live lease returns that lease when the retry carries the same tenant, run, client, lease backend, and provider, and either names no device or the device the lease binds, so a retry after a lost reply does not allocate a second one. A retry without `ttlMs` keeps the lease’s window. A retry that changes any of those fields is refused like any other reused id. The id identifies the lease: one run can hold several leases. Any other id this daemon has already given a lease, active or ended, is refused with `INVALID_ARGS` and reason `LEASE_ID_IN_USE`, and without one the daemon makes the id. Use the id the reply carries: a run that already holds a lease gets that lease back, and an older daemon ignores the requested id.

Several agents can share one proxy, and one machine, when each names its own session and follows the same `connect proxy`, `open`, commands, `close`, and `disconnect` flow. A busy device error means another agent holds the device until it closes its session or its lease expires.

Do not put the proxy endpoint, token, tenant, or provider fields in `./agent-device.json`: repository configuration accepts only project-safe automation defaults. Set the endpoint and token with `connect proxy`, user config, an explicit `--config` file, or protected CI environment variables.

## Lease by device spec

A service in front of the daemon, such as simlock, can also pick the device by OS version, Android image tag, iOS simulator mode, saved device state (baseline), and physical or virtual class. Pass `--os <version|range>`, `--image-tag <tag>`, `--device-mode <slim|full>`, `--device-baseline <name>`, or `--physical` to `open`, `install`, `reinstall`, or `uninstall`, and the CLI sends them with `--platform`, `--target`, and `--device` on the lease request. A non-blank `osVersion`, `imageTag`, `deviceMode` or `deviceBaseline` and `physical: true` name a spec key and are sent as given. An empty or blank string and `physical: false` name nothing, from the CLI, the SDK, or MCP. A value of another type (for example `physical: "yes"`) fails with `INVALID_ARGS` and `details.reason: "device-spec-invalid"`. The service validates the values themselves (for example, Android `--os` is an API level). `connect proxy` stores the spec keys it names as defaults like `--platform` and `--device`. `--target` stays the device class selector.

```bash
agent-device open MyApp --platform ios --device "iPhone 17 Pro" --os ">=26"
agent-device open MyApp --platform android --os 34 --image-tag google_apis_playstore
agent-device open MyApp --platform ios --physical --os 18.6.2
agent-device open MyApp --platform ios --device-mode full
agent-device open MyApp --platform ios --device-baseline logged-in
```

| Flag                         | Key on `agent_device.lease.allocate` | Type   |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------ | ------ |
| `--os <version\|range>`      | `osVersion`                          | string |
| `--image-tag <tag>`          | `imageTag`                           | string |
| `--device-mode <slim\|full>` | `deviceMode`                         | string |
| `--device-baseline <name>`   | `deviceBaseline`                     | string |
| `--physical`                 | `physical`                           | `true` |

With `--physical`, the service leases one of the real phones enrolled with it instead of a simulator or emulator.

A service that honours the spec returns the granted device on the lease as `lease.device`: `model`, `osVersion` (the exact OS granted), `imageTag` and `baseline` (`name` and `version`) when they apply, and `physical`. `open --json` prints it under `lease.device`. A service can also report the granted simulator mode there as `deviceMode`. A lease that reports `slim` for `--device-mode full` fails the command with reason `device-spec-unsupported`, and is released unless the daemon explicitly reported `created:false` (reuse). `slim` is best effort, so a `full` simulator can serve `--device-mode slim`.
