A lease that reports no mode is accepted, so `--device-mode` needs a service that supports the key: one that ignores it and reports no mode leases its default mode without an error.

`--device-baseline <name>` asks the service to restore a saved, prepared device state on the leased device. It is unrelated to `diff screenshot --baseline <file>`. The service reports the restored state as `lease.device.baseline` (`name` and a positive integer `version`). A new lease whose `baseline.name` is not the requested name fails the command with reason `device-spec-unsupported`, and is released unless the daemon explicitly reported `created:false` (reuse).

The daemon itself cannot pick a device by these keys, so it refuses a named key instead of ignoring it. A local daemon, or one behind a plain `agent-device proxy`, fails such a request with `UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION`, `details.reason: "device-spec-unsupported"`, and `details.keys` naming the keys it got, and records no lease. When a service returns a lease without `lease.device`, the service did not understand the spec. The CLI discards that allocate response and fails with `UNSUPPORTED_OPERATION` and `details.reason: "device-spec-unsupported"`. It releases a discarded lease unless the daemon explicitly reported `created:false` (reuse). This also applies when a grant conflicts with `--udid` or `--serial`, or when a keyless lease is replaced by the locally selected device. `details.released`, when present, reports whether the lease was released. If release throws while discarding a refused or conflicting allocation and the daemon confirmed `created:true`, the command retries that release once. A retry that releases the lease records `released:true`. Keyless fallback stops if discarding the replaced lease throws, to avoid leaving an unnamed lease while allocating another. A failed discard or rollback uses one `details.leaseRollback` shape: it names the lease and carries `released: false`, reason `LEASE_RELEASE_FAILED`, and the release error alongside the original command error. An older daemon that omits creation evidence still has refused or replaced leases released. Once its grant is bound, a later preparation failure leaves that unrecorded lease until expiry because rollback requires `created:true`. While a lease is active, a later command that names a different value for any of the five keys fails with reason `CONNECTION_DEVICE_CONFLICT`; a key the command leaves out keeps the lease’s value. Run `connect --force` to lease by another spec.

## Download captures

Remote screenshots, recordings, performance captures, and trace logs use generated output paths on the daemon. When you specify an output path through the CLI, SDK, or MCP, it selects the download destination on your machine. A recording is different: it downloads to the path named by the `record stop` request, or otherwise to the working directory with a warning. The directory of a `record start` path does not carry over; the working-directory fallback keeps only its file name. Direct RPC callers receive artifact IDs and download each result with `GET /artifacts/<id>` using the same authentication.

By default, artifacts leave the inventory after download or after 15 minutes. `AGENT_DEVICE_RETAIN_ARTIFACTS` keeps downloaded artifacts in inventory until expiry. Downloads already in progress can finish before their files are removed, including overlapping downloads of a directory archive. Closing the HTTP connection cancels that download, including directory archive preparation. Other downloads waiting for the same archive can still finish. You can retry a cancelled download while the artifact remains in inventory. Each download has a 15-minute maximum lifetime. When it reaches that limit, the daemon cancels it and cleans up after its pipeline stops.

Outside a macOS app lease, a fresh `open --save-script=<path>` records the session to a file on your machine. Each response that records an action returns a `session-script` artifact, and the client replaces the file with it. `close` returns the final script. The client writes only to the path that its own `open` named. If the file already exists, `open` fails unless you pass `--force`. The daemon must report the `script-artifacts` capability in its `/health` response; through a proxy, the upstream daemon’s health response must report it. Otherwise `open --save-script` is refused before the session starts. A session that another process closes keeps the version from the last recorded action.

A script version that is not delivered never fails the command that recorded it. The daemon may fail to write it, or this machine may fail to download or save it, for example when it is larger than 8 MiB. The command still succeeds, and the file may keep the previous version; the next recorded action or `close` delivers the full recording again. If `close` cannot deliver the final script, the session still closes and the file keeps the version from the last action. Every result that recorded a version discloses it: the CLI prints a warning and carries a typed `scriptDeliveryFailure` in `--json`, and the SDK and MCP results carry the same field.

Remote `session save-script`, `close --save-script`, `replay --save-script`, and `--save-script` in batch steps are refused. A remote `batch` updates your file once with the recording from its completed steps, including the final script when a step closes the session. If a step fails, the batch keeps that error and delivers the recording from earlier completed steps. Delivery failures add `scriptDeliveryFailure` and a warning, and your file may keep its previous version.

Direct RPC callers send `saveScript: true` with a random `meta.scriptPublicationId` of 16 to 64 letters, digits, or hyphens. Each script artifact carries that `scriptPublicationId` and a `scriptRevision` that grows with each version. For a single command, download the artifacts by ID and keep the newest. For a batch, read `scriptDeliveryReceipt` from `data` on success or `error.details` on failure: it names the `publicationId`, the optional newest full-script `version`, the optional `close.step` (a 1-based position in your submitted plan), and any typed `failures`. Download only that version, validate the close against your plan, and report the failures; do not derive delivery from step results.

Remote requests ignore `meta.cwd`. They refuse host tooling paths and `--launch-console` with reason `REMOTE_HOST_INPUT_DENIED`. They also refuse daemon host paths as `install` and `reinstall` binaries, `push` payload files, and xctrace template files. `open` targets and launch URLs cannot use the `file:` scheme. Serve local web content over HTTP(S) instead. Upload binaries with the client, send `push` payloads as inline JSON, and name xctrace templates. Omit these inputs, or use a local daemon for host tooling. Test suite artifacts also use a daemon-chosen output root.

## Human takeover

With a remote device already leased by `open`, pause mutations through the same connection:

```bash
agent-device takeover --session remote-session
```

The command runs in the foreground and keeps the hold until you press Ctrl+C. While it holds, state-changing commands fail with `DEVICE_IN_USE` and `details.reason: "human_control_active"`. Snapshots, screenshots, selector reads, logs, and other read-only diagnostics still work, the agent session stays open, and its lease does not expire from inactivity. The hold activates after mutations already in progress finish. To check or recover a hold, run `takeover status` or `takeover release <hold-id>` with the same session.

If the `takeover` process disappears, its hold expires on its own. When the last hold on the device is released or expires, the lease’s inactivity window starts over. A tenant can change only the holds owned by its own lease.

If the requesting connection disconnects while the hold waits for those mutations, the pending hold is removed and never activates. This applies to both tenant RPCs and host PUTs. An active hold lasts until its TTL runs out or you release it.

Lease-owner operations use ordinary `agent_device.command` RPCs at `POST /rpc`, with command `human_control` and positionals `["list"]`, `["put", "<hold-id>", "{\"ttlMs\":15000}"]`, or `["remove", "<hold-id>"]`. Supply the same tenant, run, client, lease, backend, provider, and device metadata as other requests. The PUT payload contains only `reason` and `ttlMs`; the server derives the target from the admitted lease. It rejects caller-supplied `scope`.

### Manage holds from the host

Automation on the device host can manage holds independently of a tenant. Read the daemon’s `httpPort` and `token` from `daemon.json` in its effective state directory, then use the loopback listener with `Authorization: Bearer <daemon-token>` or `X-Agent-Device-Token: <daemon-token>`. An HTTP listener is required. A tenant credential does not grant this capability.

```text
PUT    /admin/human-control/holds/<hold-id>
GET    /admin/human-control/holds
DELETE /admin/human-control/holds/<hold-id>
```

The host PUT body names the exact lease contention identity, including its backend and provider. Use the lease’s `deviceKey`, not a bare device ID or a display name:

```json
{
  "scope": {
    "backend": "ios-instance",
    "leaseProvider": "proxy",
    "deviceKey": "ios:mobile:<simulator-udid>"
  },
  "reason": "Human is using the VM console.",
  "ttlMs": 15000
}
```

Repeated PUT renews the hold. Omitting `ttlMs` keeps it until explicit release or daemon shutdown. Tenant RPCs cannot modify host holds. Multiple holds can coexist; mutations resume only when all holds on the device end.

Holds, like leases, do not survive a daemon restart. Reconnect and put the hold back before a person continues on the device. Takeover requires a device-scoped remote lease; it does not fence off devices across local daemons on the same host.

### Lease one macOS app to a client

A host can hand a client one macOS app instead of a device. A `macos-app` lease names that app by bundle id, optionally pinned to one process (`<bundleId>@<pid>`). Only the host allocates it, on the same loopback listener and daemon token as host holds; a tenant `lease_allocate` for `macos-app` is refused:

```text
PUT    /admin/leases/<lease-id>
GET    /admin/leases
DELETE /admin/leases/<lease-id>
```

```json
{
  "tenantId": "host-tenant",
  "runId": "run-1",
  "clientId": "client-1",
  "leaseBackend": "macos-app",
  "leaseProvider": "proxy",
  "deviceKey": "com.example.app@12345",
  "ttlMs": 300000
}
```

The lease id is 16 to 128 hex characters the host chooses. Repeating the PUT renews the lease; a PUT that names another scope for an existing id is refused. The lease stays allocated across the client’s `close` unless the body sets `retainOnClose: false`, and DELETE revokes it at once. It expires after `ttlMs` without a renewal or a client request, like any lease. A client heartbeat can shorten that window but never extend it past the `ttlMs` of the last PUT. A client cannot release it: `disconnect` drops only its local connection state, and a tenant `lease_release` is refused with `MACOS_APP_LEASE_HOST_OWNED`. The lease ends by the host’s `DELETE /admin/leases/<lease-id>`, by expiry, by daemon restart, or when a session it holds closes and the body set `retainOnClose` to false.

The client connects with a remote config that names the lease, and runs `open <bundleId>`:

```json
{
  "daemonBaseUrl": "https://<tunnel-url>",
  "daemonAuthToken": "<client-token>",
  "tenant": "host-tenant",
  "runId": "run-1",
  "clientId": "client-1",
  "leaseId": "<lease-id>",
  "leaseBackend": "macos-app",
  "leaseProvider": "proxy",
  "deviceKey": "com.example.app@12345",
  "platform": "macos"
}
```

Requests under a `macos-app` lease are limited to `open`, `close`, `snapshot`, `wait`, `find`, `get`, `is`, `click`, `fill`, `press`, `type`, `focus`, `scroll`, `screenshot`, and `batch`, plus the lease’s own heartbeat; `doctor`, `devices`, `session list` and the other inventory commands are refused too. `open` and `close` accept only the leased bundle id, only the `app` surface is allowed, screenshots capture only the app window, inputs that name a host path or a launch (`--save-script`, `--launch-url`, `--launch-console`) are refused, device selectors (`--udid`, `--serial`, `--device`, `--target`) are refused, `open` and `batch` must carry `--platform macos`, every other command must run in the session `open` created for the leased app, and a pid-pinned lease stops working when that process exits. `open` requires the daemon to run the native macOS app backend (`AGENT_DEVICE_MACOS_APP_BACKEND=native`). A refusal fails with `UNAUTHORIZED` and `details.reason: "MACOS_APP_LEASE_DENIED"`.

Responses under the lease name nothing else about the host. `open` omits the session state and log paths and the device (`device`, `id`, `kind`), a failure omits `logPath` and `diagnosticsRecord` and replaces host paths and the host name in its text with `<host-path>` and `<host>`, and a snapshot’s fallback screenshot path stays on the host; the screenshot arrives through the artifact route. The request diagnostics route is not served to a tenant that held the lease, and a daemon started with `leases.require` does not serve it at all.

These rules apply to requests made under the lease. To refuse requests that name no lease at all, start the daemon with a policy that requires one (`leases.require`, below). The proxy token is shared by every client of the proxy, so a host serving several clients through one proxy authenticates each client itself and sets each request’s tenant, session isolation, and lease before forwarding it. Embedding `@agent-device/proxy` with its `authenticate` option does the tenant and session isolation part: the proxy sends each client’s requests as the tenant `authenticate` returns. A tenant id is 1-128 letters, numbers, dots, underscores or hyphens; any other id fails the request with a 500. On `/rpc` the proxy accepts only `agent_device.command` and the `agent_device.lease.*` methods, and refuses others with a 401. Upload tickets carry the client’s own `authorization` and `x-agent-device-token` headers, or the `uploadHeaders` that `authenticate` returns, and never the daemon’s token.

## Restrict what clients can do

Start the proxy with a daemon policy to confine every client to named devices and commands. The daemon enforces the policy on every request, including `batch` steps and `replay` actions:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "devices": { "allow": [{ "udid": "<simulator-udid>" }] },
  "commands": { "deny": ["boot", "shutdown"] },
  "capabilities": { "deny": ["device-shutdown"] }
}
```

```bash
AGENT_DEVICE_DAEMON_POLICY=./policy.json agent-device proxy
```

* `devices.allow` lists the only devices clients can see (`devices`) or use. Use `udid` for Apple devices and `serial` for Android. With the native macOS backend, allowing the Mac also allows each app on it. To allow one app only, list its app device id, for example `host-macos-local:app:com.apple.textedit`. The Mac then appears in `devices`, but whole-Mac sessions stay denied.
* `commands` takes either `allow` or `deny`, not both. With `allow`, commands added in later releases stay denied. Some client-side tools reach the daemon through internal commands: allow `runtime` for Maestro flows, and `install-from-source` for remote installs.
* `capabilities.deny: ["device-shutdown"]` blocks `shutdown`, `close --shutdown`, and any other path that would shut the device down.
* `leases.require: "macos-app"` (the only accepted value) refuses every request that is not made under a `macos-app` lease or that its allow list does not cover, including requests that name no lease and inventory commands such as `doctor` and `session list`.

The daemon reads the file once at start and refuses to start if it is invalid. If a daemon is already running for the state directory with a different policy, the proxy refuses to reuse it; stop that daemon first. A denied request fails with `UNAUTHORIZED` and `details.reason: "DAEMON_POLICY_DENIED"`.

## What the proxy exposes

The proxy serves only the daemon HTTP contract: `/health`, `/rpc`, `/upload` plus resumable `/upload/*` routes, and `/artifacts/*`, with the same routes also available under `/agent-device/*`. Health checks are unauthenticated; command, upload, and artifact routes require the bearer token. `GET /artifacts` lists the caller tenant’s downloadable artifacts. An entry has `sessionName` when the daemon registered it outside a request reply, for example a recording kept when its leased session ended.

The proxy passes the daemon’s HTTP status through. Most failed upload and artifact requests answer a JSON body `{ "ok": false, "error": "...", "code": "..." }`. When the daemon writes this body, it also carries a `hint`, and `reason` when the error has one. An artifact, upload, or materialized-path id that was already consumed, has expired, or never existed answers `404` with `code: "COMMAND_FAILED"` and `reason: "RESOURCE_EXPIRED"`. A `/rpc` call that names the same id answers `404` when it does not stream progress. A call that streams progress, as the CLI does without `--json`, can already have answered `200`; its final envelope carries the failure.

Other failures answer a `4xx` or `5xx` status that depends on the route and the error. For example, invalid arguments answer `400`, a bad token answers `401`, and a human-control hold answers `423`. The proxy answers its own failures, such as an unreachable daemon, with `500` and no `reason`. The daemon and the proxy share error codes. Read `code` and `reason` to interpret an error. Do not use them to tell whether the daemon or the proxy answered.

The proxy checks the client token and forwards authorized requests with the local daemon token. Remote clients never see the daemon token.

The proxy does not forward `/admin/*`, including human-control holds. A caller on the device host must use the daemon’s loopback port and local daemon token.

## Embed the proxy in your own gateway

`agent-device proxy` is also available as a library, `@agent-device/proxy`, for gateways that front daemons on many hosts. It serves the same routes with the same token handling, but you choose the transport on both sides: it answers standard Fetch API `Request` objects, so you can host it on any HTTP server or carry requests over WebSocket, and it can reach the daemon through your own tunnel instead of HTTP. See the [package README](https://github.com/callstack/agent-device/tree/main/packages/proxy#readme) for the API.

## Compatibility

Remote clients read `/health` before sending commands and compare the daemon RPC protocol version. Keep client and proxy versions close: patch-level differences usually work, and incompatible RPC protocol versions fail before any command runs.

`/health` also reports `hostArch`, the native CPU architecture of the machine serving it: the one its simulators run by default, even when Node itself runs under Rosetta. Macs report `arm64` or `x86_64`; other hosts report `x86_64` for x64 and Node’s `process.arch` name otherwise (for example `arm64`). The top-level value describes the proxy’s own machine, so a client behind a proxy reads `upstream.hostArch` for the host that runs the simulators, for example to build only that slice of a simulator app. Older daemons omit the field. `leaseBackends` lists the lease backends the daemon admits (`macos-app` only on a macOS host); a host checks `upstream.leaseBackends` for `macos-app` before handing out a macOS app lease, and older daemons omit it.

```json
{"ok":true,"service":"agent-device-proxy","version":"0.21.39-dev","rpcProtocolVersion":3,"instanceId":"5f0c2d7e-8a41-4b7e-9c3a-2e6d1f4b8a90","hostArch":"arm64","upstream":{"ok":true,"service":"agent-device-daemon","version":"0.21.39-dev","rpcProtocolVersion":3,"instanceId":"b3e9a6c1-4d2f-4f8e-a0b7-7c5d9e1f2a34","hostArch":"arm64"}}
```

## Clean up

Run `agent-device disconnect` when you finish the remote session. Stop the tunnel and the `agent-device proxy` process only when the host should stop accepting remote clients. Restarting the proxy generates a fresh token unless you supplied `--daemon-auth-token` explicitly.

# Replay and E2E testing

Record a session as an `.ad` script, then run it again with `replay` or run a folder of scripts as an E2E suite with `test`.

`replay` has a 60-second wall-clock budget within a 90-second client timeout. Use `replay workflow.ad --timeout 300000` for a five-minute operation budget and a five-minute, 30-second client timeout. At the budget, the running step receives the same cancellation as a canceled request. When it settles, a failed replay includes `details.reason: daemon_request_timeout` and `details.timeoutMs`. The daemon and other sessions stay available if it responds to the client. An authored `close` may already have ended its session. A failed replay keeps the failing script path and line. A replay that completes every step returns success even if it settles shortly after the deadline. Cancellation does not prove that native device work has stopped. If a step ignores cancellation beyond the remaining 30 seconds, the client may report a transport timeout. For a daemon that does not respond, the client’s existing liveness check can reset it. Direct `test` runs keep their own timeout behavior.

If a resource step cannot run within replay’s budget, the error includes `details.reason: bounded_composite_resource_unsupported`, `details.shape`, `details.dispatched: no` for that step, and `details.standaloneCommandName` for a known public command. This can affect `perf`, `audio`, `record`, `trace`, and some `logs` operations. It also affects `close` when it would dispose owned resources or release a provider lease, and acquisition that would recover another session’s durable resources. Opening another app in the same session keeps its owned resource handles. An Android test IME alone is restored by authored `close`, even when restoration settles after the remaining replay time. A failed restore on a session that holds a device claim keeps the session and its claim; inspect the device, then retry `close` with the same options, leaving out `--save-script` once the script is published. A session without a claim is retired. The name is not a complete command. Inspect the failed script path and line, then run that original operation separately with its original arguments and options, the same `--session` value, and the same private CLI context. If steps remain and the report offers `resume.alternateFrom`, use it with `planDigest` after completing the refused step directly. `resume.from` retries the same bounded step and refuses it again. A final unrecorded `logs` or `audio` step leaves no replay tail to resume. Inspect completed steps before retrying; earlier steps may have changed the app. A nested `test` with an attempt timeout or `--record-video` is refused before its first attempt. Direct `test` retains its own timeout behavior. If a nested test reaches a bounded resource refusal, it stops after that attempt even when you configured retries. Other test failures can still retry. An authored `.ad` command without a resource classification fails closed with `details.shape: <command>:unclassified` and the same original-input guidance.

To run Maestro YAML flows or export `.ad` scripts to Maestro YAML, see [Run Maestro flows](/docs/run-maestro-flows).

## How it works

You work in two passes:

1. Explore: discover elements and act on refs (`snapshot` -> `click @e..` / `fill @e..`) while recording.
2. Replay: run the recorded `.ad` script with `replay` for a deterministic run.

## Record a replay script

Pass `--save-script` to `open`. When you `close` the session, the script is written:

```bash
agent-device open Settings --platform ios --session e2e --save-script
agent-device snapshot -i --session e2e
agent-device click @e13 --session e2e
agent-device close --session e2e
```

By default, the script goes to:

```text
~/.agent-device/sessions/<session>-<timestamp>.ad
```

Each recorded element step writes its target as a selector. When the element’s id is unique on the recorded screen, the step writes only that id, for example `press 'id="submit"'`. Otherwise, it writes alternatives such as role and label, joined with `||`, for example `press 'role="button" label="Submit" || label="Submit"'`.

To choose the output file, pass a path to `--save-script`:

```bash
agent-device open Settings --platform ios --session e2e --save-script ./workflows/e2e-settings.ad
```

* The path has to end in a file name. A path ending in `.`, `..`, or a bare `~` or root is refused before anything is created, because it names a directory. A trailing `/` after a file name still writes that file.
* On Windows, use a drive-letter path (`C:\recordings\journey.ad`) or a `\\server\share` path. A path relative to the current drive (`\journey.ad`) and an extended-length path (`\\?\...`) are refused on purpose, and so is a relative or `~/` path whose working directory or home has one of those forms. Paths in a pipe, `IPC$` or mailslot share are refused too.
* Missing parent directories are created, one at a time, and only once the directories above them pass the check below. Each new directory is created at mode `0700`, whatever your umask, because it holds private recordings. A destination refused before any directory is created leaves nothing behind, even where its parent was missing; a refusal after creation starts can leave the empty directories already created. A path that steps back out of a directory that does not exist yet (`private/missing/../../shared/recordings`) is refused rather than created into existence: the directories it names would be built by a rule that never judged them. A recording’s script file, local or remote, is created at exactly mode `0600`, so its own permissions open it to nobody but you. What those permissions do not settle for you is listed under the limits below.
* Every directory the write travels through must be one that no other local user can change, with one exception: the members of the group of a directory you own and left group-writable can change it. Each directory must be owned by you or by root, and apart from that exception its permissions must prevent other users from modifying entries in it. Another local user who owns such a directory, or who can write in it, can replace a directory on the path or leave a symbolic link there, and the script then lands where they choose.
* The check follows the path the way the system does, one name at a time, and judges every directory it looks a name up in. So a plain directory that is open to others cannot hide a link into a private destination (`rec -> shared/relay/sub`, where `shared/relay` is itself a link), and a link inside a link cannot hide the directory it crosses. A link written as `ln -s ../team/rec rec` is followed from the directory that holds it, and a `..` inside it is applied one step at a time. A `..` in the path you typed is applied to the directory the walk actually reached, not to the text: where `work` is a link, `work/../x` lands beside the link’s target, and that is the directory judged. A relative path such as `./workflows/journey.ad` is expanded against your working directory first, and the whole chain from the root is then checked, so a working directory that sits in ground others can write is refused too. The file is written into that same resolved directory, temp file included, so nothing is staged in a directory the check never reached. Where the check cannot reach the directory your path names, because a name inside it does not exist, the save is refused instead of writing beside the closest directory it did reach. Following more links than the system allows is refused rather than trusted.
* Every symbolic link the path follows is checked wherever it leads, at any depth, not only the ones you typed. A link is refused if another user could have placed it, or could replace it: in a directory where others may add entries, only a link you or root own, held in place by the sticky bit, is trusted. A group-writable directory you own is the exception: a link in it is followed, whoever placed it. Its own permission bits are not consulted: on Linux every link reports the same mode. Root-owned system links such as macOS `/tmp` and `/var` keep working.
* A directory you or root own may still be passed through when it carries the sticky bit (`chmod +t`) and is open to others, because that bit stops anyone but an entry’s owner or root from replacing an entry: macOS `/tmp` works this way. A sticky directory owned by somebody else is refused — both bits shield other users from its owner, not the owner from you. The script is never created *inside* a directory others may add entries to: there, anyone could create your file’s name first. A group-writable directory that you own is accepted unless you are root or it is also world-writable, so a checkout created under umask `002`, where every directory is `0775`, works as it is. Its group is your responsibility: the members can replace a directory on the path, leave a link there, or create your file’s name first. Check which group it is with `ls -ld`, because a parent directory can pass its own group on. A group-writable directory that root owns is refused unless it is sticky and only passed through, because its members could do the same. Save under a directory you own instead: only root can close such a directory to its group.
* Limits. The checks read owners, permission bits and link shape, and four things sit outside them. **They are POSIX checks**: on Windows the walk does not run at all, so owners, permission bits and link shape are not read there and a mode such as `0600` carries no Windows meaning — Windows access comes from the ACL of the directory you chose, which is outside this rule. An access control list is consulted before the permission bits, so a directory at `0700` can still grant everyone write through an ACL, and a file at `0600` can still grant everyone read; the checks do not read ACLs. On a network mount (NFS, SMB, FUSE), ownership and mode are whatever the server answers, and the user ids there are usually not the ones on this machine. A mount can also appear over a checked directory. So these checks mean that no other local user, apart from the group members of a group-writable directory you own, can steer where the recording is written on a local filesystem without ACLs on that path; they are not a promise that nobody else can read the file. On a host like that, choose a directory only you can write.
* A refused destination names the directory at fault. A local `close` fails and keeps its bytes. A remote recording keeps its success and reports `script_ancestor_untrusted` as the `scriptDeliveryFailure` cause, and the next recorded action or `close` repeats the refusal. Choose a directory you own that only you can write.
* On a local session the check guards every route that writes to a caller-named destination, not only the one you typed a path to: `open --save-script`, the close of a session, `session save-script`, `replay --save-script` and the `<name>.healed.ad` sibling it writes when you name no output for it, and `--save-script` in a batch step. Where no path is named at all, the daemon writes its own default location the way it always has, without this check.
* With a local daemon, closing an ordinary recording writes the script on the daemon host. Relative paths resolve from the daemon’s working directory. If you omit the path, the file goes in the daemon state’s `sessions` directory. Use `session save-script` while the session is open to get the output path from the CLI. When a close writes a healed replay, the Node SDK close result includes `savedScript`. On macOS and Linux, a path you name resolves parent symbolic links.
* With a remote daemon, outside a macOS app lease, the path is on your machine. The file appears when `open` returns, and each later recorded action in the session replaces it with the recording so far. `close` writes the final script there. If a process that does not share this client’s state directory closes the session, the file keeps the version from the last action.
* Check the chosen destination after a remote `open` returns. The client adds `savedScript` and its own delivery warnings when it materializes a remote response. A raw HTTP RPC response carries no `savedScript`, and only the warning for a script the daemon could not write. They reach the result of `open`, of a recorded action and of `close`, and the Node SDK close result; at the default level the CLI `open` and `close` JSON output and the Node SDK open result do not carry `savedScript`, while `close --level full` prints the full close result, `savedScript` included. A successful `batch` carries it only when its response also lists the script artifact. A batch answered only through its delivery receipt, and a failed batch, carry no `savedScript`. For a version saved fresh, on macOS and Linux that path resolves symbolic links, and on Windows it can include a junction. A repeated version reports the stored absolute destination instead: relative and `~` paths resolved and trailing separators removed, with parent links not resolved.
* While the client still holds the recording’s active record, an equal or older version is reported with that stored destination, without fetching it or checking the file again, and with no warning. If that file is missing while the session is still recording, the next recorded action or `close` writes the full recording to the destination again. A final `close` ends the recording. If that delivery fails, later actions cannot recover the file: record again to the original `open` destination: reuse your original `open` command, with its app, URL and device arguments, with `--save-script=<path> --force`; a bare `--save-script` would pick a new file name. The hint of a refusal for an existing file names those arguments with the path quoted for a POSIX shell (in PowerShell, write an apostrophe in the path as two apostrophes inside single quotes); for a path with a newline or another C0 or C1 control character, it names `<path>` instead.
* A bare remote `open --save-script` writes `recording-<timestamp>.ad` in your working directory.
* If the probe finds an existing entry, `open` fails unless you pass `--force`. If the probe cannot read the entry or an entry appears later, `open` can succeed. Without `--force`, the first delivery creates the file exclusively, preserving any existing entry. If delivery cannot save the script, the result includes `scriptDeliveryFailure` and a warning. With `--force`, the first delivery can replace the entry. After the first save, the session replaces the file on each update.
* Remote `session save-script`, `close --save-script`, `replay --save-script`, and `--save-script` in batch steps are refused.
* A remote `batch` updates your file once with the recording from its completed steps, including the final script when a step closes the session. If a step fails, the batch keeps that error and delivers the recording from earlier completed steps. A delivery failure adds `scriptDeliveryFailure` and a warning; your file may still hold the previous version.
* The remote daemon must report the `script-artifacts` capability in its `/health` response. Through a proxy, the upstream daemon’s health response must report it. Otherwise `open --save-script` fails before the app opens.
* For a bare file name that could be read as another argument, use `--save-script=workflow.ad` or a path-like value such as `./workflow.ad`.

## `.ad` line grammar

A `.ad` line is the CLI spelling of one command: `<command> [positional ...] [flag ...]`. Whitespace separates tokens, so a value with a space needs quotes.

```sh
open "com.example.app" --relaunch
scroll down --until 'id="far-button"'
press id="far-button"
wait 'label="Order summary"' 5000
close
```

* A token quoted with `"` or `'` is one argument. Single quotes keep a `"` literal, so `'id="far-button"'` and `"id=\"far-button\""` are the same selector — write whichever matches how you typed the command at the shell.
* Values in double quotes are JSON strings, so escape `\\`, `\"`, `\t`, and `\n`. Values in single quotes are literal, as at the shell: a backslash keeps its own character, and the only escape is `\'` for an apostrophe.
* A script line keeps only the flags that command records; CLI-only spellings and per-request options are not part of a step. The common flags a script does not carry are `--settle`, `--verify`, `scroll --pixels`/`--duration-ms`, and the device-selection flags (`--platform`, `--serial`, `--device`).
* `help <command>` prints the flags each command accepts. `help scripting` prints this grammar.

To reach an off-screen element, use a stop condition rather than a fixed scroll amount. A fixed amount passes on one screen size and fails on another:

```sh
# repeats until the element is on screen
scroll down --until 'id="checkout-submit"'
# one gesture, viewport-relative
scroll down 0.8
# run to the end of the content
scroll bottom
```

A `#` only starts a comment at the beginning of a line. A scroll line carries `--until` and keeps its distance as a positional (`scroll down 0.8 --until <selector>`). `wait` carries `--raw`, `--depth <n>`, and `--scope <selector|@ref>` to choose the capture its target is read from. Scripts use only these long spellings: the `-d`/`-s` CLI aliases are not flags in a script, so a hand-written line such as `wait text -s so funny` still waits for that literal text.

## Run replay

```bash
agent-device replay ~/.agent-device/sessions/e2e-2026-02-09T12-00-00-000Z.ad --session e2e-run
```

* Replay reads `.ad` scripts.

* The CLI reads script paths on your machine and sends the script, with the Maestro `runFlow` includes it can resolve and read, to the daemon. An include it cannot read is left out, and the run fails if it reaches that include. The same `replay` or `test` command works against a local or a remote daemon without copying files. A script that doesn’t exist on your machine fails at once, naming the path you typed.

* A script that does not end in `close` leaves its session open. For a script that does end in `close`, pass `--keep-session` to skip only that final action and keep working in the same session:

  ```bash
  agent-device replay ./checkout.ad --session e2e-run --keep-session
  agent-device snapshot -i --session e2e-run
  ```

  Earlier `close` actions still run. `test` does not accept the flag because each suite attempt cleans up its own session.

* `press`, `click`, and `longpress` steps do not wait for a missing target to appear. If a screen needs time to load, add an explicit wait before the interaction, such as `wait 'label="Continue"' 5000`. Covered, off-screen, and ambiguous targets fail as they do in live commands.

* When the target is missing, replay stops with `REPLAY_DIVERGENCE`. For a step recorded with a target annotation (the `# agent-device:target-v1` line above it), `error.details.divergence.kind` is `selector-miss` and the step is never sent. For a step without an annotation, `error.details.reason` is `selector_not_found`, as for a live command.

* A step whose read names one element (`is` with a predicate other than `exists`/`absent`, or `get attrs`) that reaches dispatch with an ambiguous selector fails with `AMBIGUOUS_MATCH` as the divergence cause — the same code the live command reports, so an ambiguous recorded screen is not replayed as a missing one. An annotated step can also stop earlier, before the command runs: when pre-dispatch target binding cannot confirm the recorded identity (its identity set has more than one member with no sibling or viewport signal isolating one, or no fresh snapshot can be captured to verify against), the divergence cause is `IDENTITY_UNVERIFIABLE` instead. Both codes say the recorded screen changed; only `AMBIGUOUS_MATCH` proves your selector matched more than one element.

## Run a lightweight `.ad` suite

```bash
agent-device test ./workflows
agent-device test "./workflows/**/*.ad" --platform android
agent-device test ./workflows --timeout 60000 --retries 1
agent-device test ./workflows --artifacts-dir ./tmp/agent-device-artifacts
agent-device test ./workflows --reporter default --reporter junit:./tmp/junit.xml
```

* `test` discovers `.ad` files from files, directories, or globs and runs them serially.
* Quote relative globs to expand them on the caller from its working directory, including when the directory name contains glob characters such as `[` or `{`. A missing file input without glob characters reports an error.
* The `context platform=...` header inside each `.ad` file decides which platform that file runs on.
* `--platform` filters which files run; with a filter, files without a `context platform=` header are skipped. When filtering leaves no runnable sources, the no-match error reports how many sources were skipped for having no `context platform=` header versus how many declared another platform. Add the header to run a file under a filter, or omit `--platform` and let the selected device decide.
* Set `context timeout=...` and `context retries=...` per script; CLI flags override them. Retries are capped at `3`, and duplicate keys in the context header fail fast instead of silently overriding each other.
* By default, suite artifacts are written under `.agent-device/test-artifacts/<run-id>/...`. Each attempt writes `replay.ad`, `result.txt`, and `replay-timing.ndjson`. Failed attempts also keep copied logs and artifact files when the replay produced them.
* Copied diagnostic artifacts receive numbered filenames when their names collide with another artifact, a replay source, timing trace, or attempt manifest. `result.txt` lists the retained names in `copiedArtifacts`.
* `replay-timing.ndjson` records attempt, cleanup, and per-step start/stop events with durations. Upload it from CI even for passing runs when comparing local and CI performance.
* When an attempt hits its timeout, it is marked failed and the replay gets a short grace period to stop before the session is cleaned up.
* The default text reporter streams live progress on stderr while a suite runs, then prints the final summary, failed tests, and passed-on-retry flaky tests. Use `--verbose` to include step traces in completed-test progress output.
* The default reporter prints a `Warnings:` section after the summary when any test accumulated composable warnings — for example a Maestro step with `optional: true` that was skipped — whether that test passed or failed. A failing `replay` run repeats the warnings it accumulated as `Warning:` lines after the error. `--json` carries the same strings in each test result’s `warnings` array.
* `--reporter` is repeatable. Built-ins are `default` for the console summary and `junit:<path>` for JUnit XML. Passing any explicit reporter list replaces the implicit default reporter, so include `--reporter default` when you also want terminal output. `--report-junit <path>` is an alias for `--reporter junit:<path>`.
* JUnit reports preserve legal Unicode and whitespace, and replace characters forbidden by XML 1.0 (such as terminal ESC or NUL) with `U+FFFD` (`�`) so CI parsers can read the report. JSON and other reporters retain the original suite values.
* When `--fail-fast` and retries are both set, the current test still consumes its retries before the suite stops.

### Custom test reporters

A custom reporter formats suite output. It runs in the local CLI process, not the daemon, and can render both live progress and the final result.

```bash
agent-device test ./workflows --reporter ./scripts/replay-reporter.mjs
```

A reporter module can export a reporter object, `reporter`, `createReporter`, or a default factory. Factories receive a load context. Reporter hooks receive replay test objects and an IO context with `stdout` and `stderr` streams:

scripts/replay-reporter.mjs

```js
import fs from 'node:fs';
import path from 'node:path';


export default function createReporter(loadContext) {
  return {
    name: 'summary-file',
    onTestStep(test, context) {
      context.stderr.write(`running ${test.file} ${test.stepIndex}/${test.stepTotal}\n`);
    },
    onSuiteEnd(suite, context) {
      context.stdout.write(`finished ${suite.total} tests\n`);
      fs.mkdirSync('./tmp', { recursive: true });
      fs.writeFileSync(
        path.join('./tmp', 'report.txt'),
        JSON.stringify(
          {
            total: suite.total,
            passed: suite.passed,
            failed: suite.failed,
            modulePath: loadContext.modulePath,
          },
          null,
          2,
        ),
        'utf8',
      );
    },
    getExitCode(suite) {
      return suite.failed > 0 ? 1 : 0;
    },
  };
}
```

For a live terminal reporter that prints each completed test as an emoji, title, and duration:

scripts/emoji-reporter.mjs

```js
export default {
  name: 'emoji-status',
  onTestResult(test, context) {
    const icon = test.status === 'pass' ? '✓' : test.status === 'fail' ? '⨯' : '-';
    const title = test.title?.trim() || test.file;
    const duration =
      typeof test.durationMs === 'number' ? ` ${(test.durationMs / 1000).toFixed(2)}s` : '';


    context.stderr.write(`${icon} ${title}${duration}\n`);
  },
};
```

TypeScript reporters use the same object shape; compile them to JavaScript before passing them to `--reporter`:

```ts
const createReporter = () => ({
  name: 'typed-reporter',
  onSuiteStart(suite, context) {
    context.stderr.write(`starting ${suite.runnable} tests\n`);
  },
  onTestResult(test, context) {
    context.stderr.write(`${test.status} ${test.title ?? test.file}\n`);
  },
  onSuiteEnd(suite) {
    // Write artifacts, annotations, or summaries from suite.
  },
});


export default createReporter;
```

The CLI loads reporter modules with Node dynamic `import()`. Use `.mjs` or `.js` files at runtime; for TypeScript, compile the reporter to JavaScript before passing it to `--reporter`. Loading `.ts` files directly depends on Node’s type-stripping behavior and is not part of the supported reporter contract.

The live hooks `onSuiteStart`, `onTestStart`, `onTestStep`, and `onTestResult` run while the suite is running; reporters do not receive generic command progress. Live hooks run as events arrive and are not awaited, so keep their work synchronous and move anything async to `onSuiteEnd`, which the CLI awaits before exiting. `onSuiteEnd` receives the final suite result. `getExitCode` can only raise the suite exit code, never lower it: the highest reporter-provided code wins and failed tests still exit with `1` when no reporter raises it further, so a reporter cannot mask a failing suite. Return an integer from `0` to `255`, or `undefined` to leave the exit code unchanged. Other values fail with `INVALID_ARGS`; in particular, codes such as `256` are rejected before they can wrap to a successful process exit.

## Parametrise `.ad` scripts

Substitute `${VAR}` tokens in `.ad` scripts using values from the CLI, shell env, script-local `env` directives, or built-ins.

```sh
context platform=android
env APP_ID=settings
env WAIT_SHORT=500


open ${APP_ID} --relaunch
wait ${WAIT_SHORT}
click "label=${APP_ID}"
```

### Precedence

| Source                       | Priority | Example                                                                 |
| ---------------------------- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| CLI `-e KEY=VALUE`           | highest  | `agent-device test flow.ad -e APP_ID=demo`                              |
| Shell env prefixed `AD_VAR_` |          | `AD_VAR_APP_ID=demo agent-device test flow.ad` (imported as `APP_ID`)   |
| Script `env KEY=VALUE`       |          | `env APP_ID=settings` in header                                         |
| Built-ins                    | runtime  | `AD_PLATFORM`, `AD_SESSION`, `AD_FILENAME`, `AD_DEVICE`, `AD_ARTIFACTS` |

### Built-ins

`replay` and `test` provide these built-ins in the reserved `AD_*` namespace.

* `AD_PLATFORM` - matches `context platform=...` or the selected platform when available
* `AD_SESSION` - active session name
* `AD_FILENAME` - path of the running `.ad` file
* `AD_DEVICE` - device identifier (when `--device` is set)
* `AD_ARTIFACTS` - attempt artifacts directory (when running under `test`)

User-defined keys starting with `AD_` are rejected in `env`, `-e`, and shell imports such as `AD_VAR_AD_FOO`, so built-ins cannot be overridden.

Substitution happens inside parsed string values. It does not create extra arguments, so quote selectors or text values that contain spaces:

```sh
env SETTINGS="label=Account || label=Profile"
click "${SETTINGS}"
```

### Fallback and escape

```sh
wait ${WAIT_MS:-500}
```

`${VAR:-default}` yields `default` when `VAR` is unset.

```sh
echo "Price: \${APP}"
```

`\${APP}` emits a literal `${APP}` with no substitution.

### Recipes

Run one flow against two app variants in CI:

```sh
agent-device test ./flows/login.ad -e APP_ID=com.example.debug
agent-device test ./flows/login.ad -e APP_ID=com.example.release
```

Tune timings locally without editing the script:

```sh
AD_VAR_WAIT_SHORT=2000 agent-device replay ./flow.ad
```

Extract a reusable selector. Before:

```sh
click "label=Account || label=Profile || label=User"
wait 500
click "label=Account || label=Profile || label=User"
```

After:

```sh
env SETTINGS="label=Account || label=Profile || label=User"


click "${SETTINGS}"
wait 500
click "${SETTINGS}"
```

Quote `${VAR}` inside selector expressions so the whole expression is treated as a single argument.

### Notes

* `AD_VAR_*` values come from the shell that runs the CLI, so they apply the same way whether the daemon runs locally or remotely.
* Fallbacks do not nest: `${A:-${B}}` is not supported.
* An unresolved `${VAR}` fails with a `file:line` reference, so a misspelled variable name stops the run.

## Replay divergence and resume

A failing `replay`/`test` step returns a structured `REPLAY_DIVERGENCE` error. The report is size-bounded and redacted, and carries:

* **`step`** — the 1-based plan index and its source file/line (through Maestro `runFlow` includes).
* **`screen`** — a fresh post-failure snapshot digest with actionable refs, or `unavailable` with a reason/hint when capture failed or was sparse (never a stale tree).
* **`suggestions`** — up to 5 ranked, re-resolved candidates for the failing selector (id match ranks above role+label, which ranks above label-only), each with a `basis` you can inspect before acting. For a verified `target-v1` annotation, equally strong candidates in the recorded scroll region rank first; document order breaks remaining ties.
* **`resume`** — whether and how to continue without re-running the script from the top.

```jsonc
{
  "code": "REPLAY_DIVERGENCE",
  "details": {
    "divergence": {
      "step": { "index": 4, "source": { "path": "flow.ad", "line": 6 } },
      "screen": {
        "state": "available",
        "refsGeneration": 3,
        "refs": [
          /* ... */
        ],
      },
      "suggestions": [{ "selector": "id=\"auth_continue\"", "basis": "id" }],
      "resume": { "allowed": true, "from": 4, "planDigest": "…64 hex chars…" },
    },
  },
}
```

Text output prints a compact summary of the same fields; `--json`/MCP carry the full object.

## Resume a failed replay

During a repair armed with `replay --save-script`, diagnostic reads stay out of the healed script. To keep a corrective read, pass `--record` on that invocation, or `record: true` in that SDK/MCP call. `--record` is per-invocation only: the config key `record` and `AGENT_DEVICE_RECORD` were removed, and a config file or environment still naming them fails with migration guidance. Authored replay observations are retained automatically.

`replay --from <n> --plan-digest <sha256>` resumes **at** plan step `n`, not after it, skipping `1..n-1` without executing them. Both flags come from a divergence report’s `resume` field — `from` is the failed step, `planDigest` is the digest of the exact unchanged plan that produced it.

Choose one recovery workflow:

1. **Change the replay script.** Review the suggestion, edit the selector or include, then run a fresh full `replay ./flow.ad`. The old digest is intentionally invalid after any plan edit; do not combine it with the edited script. A later divergence supplies a new digest.
2. **Keep the replay plan unchanged.** Repair app/device state so the reported failed step can succeed when retried, then resume with the report’s unchanged `from` and `planDigest`. If you manually complete the failed action itself, the reported `from` will execute it again; only do that when repeating the action is safe.

The unchanged-plan resume loop is:

1. Run `replay ./flow.ad`. On failure, read `resume` from the divergence.
2. Leave the script, includes, platform, and target unchanged. Repair app state yourself so the failed step can be retried safely. Resume does not restore app state; it only skips the earlier steps.
3. `replay ./flow.ad --from <resume.from> --plan-digest <resume.planDigest>`.

```bash
agent-device replay ./flow.ad
# ... REPLAY_DIVERGENCE, resume: { allowed: true, from: 4, planDigest: "ab12...“ }
# (repair app state on the device)
agent-device replay ./flow.ad --from 4 --plan-digest ab12...
```

For how `--from` counts steps in a Maestro flow, see [Resume a failed Maestro flow](/docs/run-maestro-flows#resume-a-failed-maestro-flow).

Passing `--plan-digest` that no longer matches the current script — because you edited it, an include changed, or platform-conditioned expansion differs — fails `INVALID_ARGS` before any action; run a fresh full replay to get a new digest. `--from` is `replay`-only; `test` rejects it (a suite run must stay full and deterministic).

## `--update`/`-u`

`--update`/`-u` does not rewrite `.ad` files. The flag is accepted and does nothing: every replay divergence carries ranked `suggestions` whether or not you pass it. Review a suggestion, then edit the `.ad` file yourself if it’s right. [ADR 0012](https://github.com/callstack/agent-device/blob/main/docs/adr/0012-interactive-replay.md) explains why replay does not rewrite scripts automatically.

## Troubleshooting

* Replay fails after UI/layout changes:
  * Read the divergence report’s `suggestions` and repair the selector by hand; there is no automated rewrite. Because the edit changes the plan digest, run a fresh full replay instead of using the old resume flags.
* Repeated re-runs are slow or the app is stateful, but the script is still correct:
  * Repair app state and resume with the unchanged `--from`/`--plan-digest`. See [Resume a failed replay](#resume-a-failed-replay).
* Replay file parse error:
  * Validate quoting in `.ad` lines (unclosed double quotes are rejected). A selector with a space needs quotes, and `help scripting` states how each quote form decodes.
* A replay passes on one device size and fails on another because a target was off screen:
  * The script used a fixed `scroll` amount. Replace it with the stop condition, `scroll down --until <selector>`, which repeats until the element is actually on screen.
* A `press` or `click` step fails because its target was not found, but the element is on the screenshot:
  * A `selector-miss` divergence means the target was absent from the captured accessibility tree. Check the selector for this build and whether the app exposes the element to accessibility. Add a `wait` step for a landmark on a loading screen before the press.

# Revyl

> Drive Revyl cloud iOS simulators and Android emulators with agent-device.

Use [Revyl](https://revyl.com) to run agent-device on hosted iOS simulators and Android emulators. You need a Revyl API key and the `@agent-device/revyl` plugin. Revyl issues keys to its customers; a partner integration gets one through Revyl’s partner program.

Revyl is not a WebDriver grid. agent-device rents a device from Revyl’s execution API and drives it through the same device-proxy actions Revyl’s own clients use, so there is no Appium session, no `lt:options` capability set, and no Appium log to read afterwards.

## Install the plugin

```bash
agent-device plugins add @agent-device/revyl
```

The plugin is an optional npm package installed under `AGENT_DEVICE_HOME`. After you add or update it, close open sessions and run `agent-device daemon stop` with the state directory you use; the next device command loads the plugin.

## Set credentials and connect

```bash
export REVYL_API_KEY=...
export AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION=checkout-ios
agent-device connect revyl --platform ios
```

`connect` authenticates against the Revyl backend with one cheap request and saves the profile. It does not rent a device: Revyl picks and boots a device when the first device command allocates the lease, usually `open`. `--device` and `--provider-os-version` are optional; without them Revyl picks from its own pool and reports a device agent-device then uses. A model or OS version Revyl has no device for is reported when the session starts, not by `connect`.

To start faster, leave `--device` and `--provider-os-version` unset, so Revyl can pick a simulator that is already running. A session can take longer to start when Revyl also installs the app on the device. Start the session early and keep it open between steps. To relaunch the app, run `open` again on the same session instead of `disconnect` and `connect`.

Without `--provider-app`, the device starts with no app. Run `install` to put a local build on it:

```bash
agent-device install com.example.app ./build/Example.app
```

`install` uploads the build to the session’s storage, and Revyl installs it from there. For iOS, pass a simulator `.app` directory, or a `.zip`, `.tar.gz`, or `.tgz` of one. A device `.ipa` does not run on a simulator. For Android, pass the `.apk`.

`install-from-source` takes a build from a URL or a CI artifact instead. agent-device downloads it, reads the app’s identifier from it, and installs it the same way:

```bash
agent-device install-from-source https://builds.example.com/app-debug.apk --platform android
```

`reinstall` refuses. Revyl cannot uninstall an app, and installing over one keeps its data, so it cannot give you the clean app `reinstall` promises. Run `install` to update the build in place, or start a new session for a clean app.

`--provider-app` installs a hosted build when the device starts instead. It must be a public HTTPS URL that Revyl can download: the zipped `.app` for iOS, or the `.apk` for Android.

`open` takes the app’s installed bundle identifier or package name, not the file name in that URL. Run these commands in the same shell, so they use the `AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION` you exported:

```bash
agent-device open com.example.app
agent-device snapshot -i
agent-device click 'label="Continue"'
agent-device close
agent-device disconnect
```

`close` ends the app on the device. `disconnect`, and any daemon shutdown, ends the Revyl session, so the device is returned. While the session is connected, the plugin tells Revyl it is still in use once a minute, so a pause between commands does not end it. If the process exits without disconnecting, Revyl releases the session after five idle minutes.

## What works on a Revyl session

A Revyl session runs the commands that reach a device through Revyl’s device actions:

* `snapshot` and `screenshot`. iOS reads the simulator’s accessibility tree and Android reads its uiautomator dump, so `snapshot -i`, `--json`, and label and selector targeting work the same way they do on a local device.
* `click`, `press`, `double tap`, `longpress`, and `fill` by point or by snapshot reference, and `scroll` by direction. `scroll` sends one drag of the planned finger path, so `--pixels` and `--amount` mean the same distance they mean on a local device. `scroll --duration-ms` sets how long the drag takes, from 1 to 10000 ms, when Revyl’s worker supports it. An older worker picks the speed itself, so there the flag refuses rather than running the drag at a speed nobody chose. `fill --delay-ms` is paced by typing one character per pause.
* `install` of a local build, `install-from-source` from a URL or CI artifact, `open` with the app’s bundle identifier or package name, `open` with a deep link or URL, and `close` for the app the session opened.
* `home`, and `back` on Android. iOS has no system back button; click the app’s own back control.
* `orientation`. A worker that reports precise orientation, as Revyl’s Android emulators do, rotates to all four sides. Any other worker, such as an iOS simulator, rotates to `portrait` and `landscape-left` only, and refuses the other two. Neither releases the rotation lock, so `orientation auto` refuses.
* `settings appearance` (`light`, `dark`, or `toggle`), `settings location set <lat> <lon>`, `settings permission`, and `settings clear-app-state`. On iOS, `settings reset-keychain` also works. Revyl starts every Android device with location services on, so `settings location on` succeeds there without changing anything, and `settings location off` refuses, because Revyl cannot switch location services off. On iOS, `settings location on|off` refuses; grant the app location with `settings permission grant location`. `settings permission` refuses `location-always`, `contacts-limited`, and `--mode limited`. Revyl’s iOS simulators refuse `camera` and `notifications`.

The plugin refuses every other command with a reason that names the substitute. It does not report a refused command as a success:

* `type` refuses and points at `fill`, because Revyl enters text at a point rather than into the field the platform happens to focus.
* `swipe` and `gesture` refuse. Use `scroll`, which plans the path itself and sends one drag.
* `keyboard`, `clipboard`, `alert`, `fold`, `telephony`, and `tv-remote` are not supported.
* The other `settings` refuse: `wifi`, `airplane`, `mobile-data`, `bluetooth`, `animations`, `text-size`, `faceid`, `touchid`, and `fingerprint`. Revyl’s devices refuse airplane mode, and the worker has no action for the rest.
* `reinstall` refuses, as described above.
* `uninstall`, `apps`, `push`, `logs`, `network dump`, `artifacts`, and `recordings` are not supported by this version of the plugin.
* `port reverse` is unavailable. Publish your app server at a public HTTPS URL instead of pointing Metro at `localhost`.

`devices` lists only the device your own session rented.

## Run it in CI

The plugin reads only `REVYL_API_KEY` and the optional `REVYL_API_URL`, so one secret is enough. Name the session once for the job, so that every step reaches the same connection:

```yaml
env:
  AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION: revyl-${{ github.run_id }}
steps:
- run: npm install -g agent-device && agent-device plugins add @agent-device/revyl
- run: agent-device connect revyl --platform android --provider-app "$APP_URL"
- run: agent-device open com.example.app && agent-device snapshot -i
- run: agent-device disconnect
  if: always()
```

Keep the `disconnect`: it is what ends the rented device when a run fails before `close`.

A running daemon keeps the `REVYL_API_KEY` it started with. If your shell holds a different one, the first command that allocates a device refuses before it rents one. Run `agent-device daemon stop` with the same `--state-dir`, then rerun the command. See [Change credentials while the daemon runs](/docs/device-clouds#change-credentials-while-the-daemon-runs).

To use a staging or private Revyl backend, set `REVYL_API_URL` to its origin, for example `https://backend.example.com`. It must be HTTPS; plain HTTP is accepted only for a loopback address, which is what a local fake of the API is for.

## Use it from JavaScript

Install the plugin package as a dependency of your host and pass it to a host you start yourself. `startAgentDevice()` runs the daemon in your process and registers the plugin objects you hand it, so no `plugins add` step and no `REVYL_API_KEY` in the environment are needed:

```ts
import { createAgentDeviceClient, startAgentDevice } from 'agent-device';
import revyl from '@agent-device/revyl';


const host = await startAgentDevice({
  stateDir: './.my-app/agent-device-state',
  plugins: [revyl({ apiKey: 'your-api-key', apiUrl: 'https://backend.example.com' })],
});


const scope = {
  tenant: 'revyl',
  runId: process.env.GITHUB_RUN_ID ?? 'local-run',
  leaseBackend: 'ios-instance',
  leaseProvider: 'revyl',
} as const;


const lease = await host.client.leases.allocate({
  ...scope,
  platform: 'ios',
  providerApp: 'https://apps.example.com/MyApp-simulator.zip',
});
const client = createAgentDeviceClient({ ...host.clientConfig, ...scope, leaseId: lease.leaseId });


try {
  await client.apps.open({ app: 'com.example.app' });
  await client.capture.snapshot({ interactiveOnly: true });
  await client.interactions.click({ selector: 'label="Continue"' });
} finally {
  // Releasing the lease ends the Revyl session, so a failure cannot leave a device rented.
  // The inner finally closes the host even when the release itself fails; otherwise the embedded
  // daemon stays alive and nothing retries the release.
  try {
    await host.client.leases.release({ ...scope, leaseId: lease.leaseId });
  } finally {
    await host.close();
  }
}
```

`apiUrl` is optional and only needed for a staging or private Revyl backend. Leaving both out makes the plugin read `REVYL_API_KEY` from the environment, which is also the only path a CLI or MCP session takes when the daemon loads the plugin from the plugin store.

## Troubleshoot

* `UNAUTHORIZED` from `connect`: `REVYL_API_KEY` is not a key that backend accepts, or `REVYL_API_URL` points at a different environment than the key was issued for.
* A start that never becomes ready reports `provider-not-ready` or `provider-start-failed` and stops the run it started, so a failed `open` does not leave a rented device. Retry, then check that Revyl has a device of the requested model and OS version.
* `snapshot` on iOS can fail with HTTP 500 while the simulator’s accessibility service briefly returns nothing. The plugin retries the read; if it still fails, run `snapshot` again.
* A device that Revyl released while your session was open reports `provider-session-gone`. Run `close` and `open` again to rent a fresh one.
* An `open` still waiting for its device when its lease is released reports `provider-lease-releasing`. That lease is ending; run `open` again, which allocates a new lease and rents a fresh device. An `open` that names no deadline stops waiting for a device after 370 s.

# Run Maestro flows

`agent-device` runs a subset of Maestro YAML flows on iOS and Android, and exports `.ad` scripts to Maestro YAML. This is a compatibility layer, not full Maestro support:

* Only the commands and fields in [Supported subset](#supported-subset) run. Anything else fails with source context instead of being skipped.
* Flows run on iOS and Android only.
* `runScript`, `evalScript`, and JavaScript conditions execute flow code on the machine running the agent-device daemon, without a security sandbox. Remote flows refuse these scripts. Run them only in trusted local flows.

For recording and replaying native `.ad` scripts, see [Replay and E2E testing](/docs/replay-e2e).

## Run a Maestro flow

Pass `--maestro` to `replay` or `test`:

```bash
agent-device replay ./flow.yaml --maestro --platform ios --session e2e-run
agent-device test ./maestro-flows --maestro --platform android --artifacts-dir ./tmp/maestro-artifacts
```

Keep the target binding, such as `--platform ios`, on the `replay` or `test` command. `agent-device help maestro` prints the same subset and boundaries as this page.

## Supported subset

* Flows: `launchApp` (with `clearState`, `permissions`, and Apple-only launch arguments; `permissions` apply after state clearing but before launch, and a `launchApp` without `permissions` touches nothing — there is no silent `all: allow` default); `setPermissions` (mid-flow permission grants, denials, and resets; `all` resolves in the backend — each simctl privacy service on iOS, the declared permissions on Android — with specific entries overriding after it); `runFlow` file/inline; `runFlow.when` and `repeat.while` conditions (`platform`, `visible`, `notVisible`, and `true`, all re-evaluated before every `repeat` iteration); `onFlowStart`/`onFlowComplete`; `repeat` with `times`, `while`, or both; and retry.
* Interactions: `tapOn`, `doubleTapOn`, `longPressOn`, `inputText` on the focused element, `eraseText` (up to 10000 characters), `openLink`, `hideKeyboard`, basic `pressKey`, and `back`; selector targets poll until available and support recursive `index`, `childOf`, `above`, `below`, `leftOf`, `rightOf`, `containsChild`, `containsDescendants`, points, and `optional`; outer command labels are metadata, not target selectors.
* Assertions and navigation: `assertVisible`, `assertNotVisible`, `assertTrue` (literal values and `${VAR}` lookups only; `""`, `"false"`, `"0"`, `"null"`, and `"undefined"` are falsy, everything else is truthy), `extendedWaitUntil`, `scroll`, `scrollUntilVisible`, absolute/percentage/target `swipe`, `takeScreenshot`, `waitForAnimationToEnd`, `clearState`, `stopApp`, and `killApp` (system-initiated process death: `am kill` on ADB-backed Android devices, which refuse a foreground target with `android-kill-requires-background-app` — background the app first, for example `pressKey: Home` — and fail a target whose process survives with `android-kill-process-survived`; iOS, Limrun, and WebDriver-provider backends run it as `stopApp`).
* Scripts: ordered `runScript` file/env scripts with `http.post`, `json`, and `output` variables; `evalScript` inline expressions run flow-scoped JavaScript and write `output.*` leaves for later steps.

## Boundaries

* Permissions: every entry is one `settings permission` call, applied in order with `all` first; the step stops at the first entry the selected platform refuses, earlier entries stay applied, and the error names what landed. Android’s only allow level is while-in-use, so `location: inuse` and `location: never` mean `allow` and `deny` there, while `location: always` and `photos: limited` are Apple-only and fail. On iOS, which service a runtime changes is `simctl privacy`’s own verdict: current runtimes refuse a targeted `notifications` change and leave notifications untouched under `all`.
* Runtime: iOS and Android only; `launchApp.clearState` and standalone `clearState` support Android and iOS simulators, launch arguments are Apple-only (a map-form argument key gains a leading `-` unless its value is a boolean, as in Maestro), and other standalone device utility/state commands are unsupported.
* Expressions: `evalScript` and condition `true:` fields (`runFlow.when` and `repeat.while` share one evaluator) are evaluated as JavaScript (flow `env` and prior `output` leaves are string-typed); a `true:` field that is a boolean, a `maestro.platform` comparison, or plain literal text after `${VAR}` lookups is decided without JavaScript, with the `assertTrue` falsy table for literal text. Other fields stay literal or `${VAR}` lookup-only — `assertTrue` supports literals and bare lookups, and other expression-shaped payloads fail loud.
* Environment: flow `env` is the default, `AD_VAR_*` overrides it, and CLI `-e KEY=VALUE` wins over both; override keys follow the flow variable grammar (mixed case and dots allowed), and `AD_*` stays reserved.
* Failure diagnostics: resolved targets and `runFlow` paths are rendered, while `inputText` payloads remain hidden; do not place secrets in diagnostic identifiers.
* Trust: `runScript`, `evalScript`, and JavaScript condition `true:` fields execute flow scripts via `node:vm`, which is not a security sandbox. `runScript` runs in a daemon child process with a 30 s script budget. It may make `http.post` network requests (30 s each, response bodies up to 8 MiB), and its output keys cannot contain a dot. Remote flows refuse `runScript` before reading its file, including files supplied in the replay bundle, and refuse `evalScript` and `true:` fields that need JavaScript. Run these scripts only in trusted local flows. Local `runScript` paths refer to the daemon filesystem: relative paths resolve from the containing flow, and absolute paths and symlinks are allowed.
* Errors and tracking: unsupported commands and fields fail with source context when available; open a focused issue only when implementation work is planned.
* Remote screenshots: `takeScreenshot` uses a daemon-generated path and reports that path in `artifactPaths`. The flow cannot choose a file destination on the daemon host. Animation waits and tap retry comparisons use temporary screenshots that are removed after comparison.
* Session takeover: `--keep-session` is a native `.ad` replay option and is rejected for Maestro YAML.

[ADR 0015](https://github.com/callstack/agent-device/blob/main/docs/adr/0015-direct-maestro-engine.md) lists the deliberate deviations from Maestro. If a missing feature matters for your suite, [open a focused issue](https://github.com/callstack/agent-device/issues/new) with a small flow snippet.

## Resume a failed Maestro flow

A failed Maestro step returns the same replay divergence report as an `.ad` script, including the resume information, and `replay --from <n> --plan-digest <sha256>` resumes it the same way. See [Resume a failed replay](/docs/replay-e2e#resume-a-failed-replay) for the workflow.

For Maestro flows, `--from` counts steps in the top-level plan. A `runFlow` with no condition, or with a condition that resolves before the run, is flattened into its commands (or dropped when the condition is false). A control step decided at run time (`runFlow`, `repeat`, or `retry`) counts as one step, and you cannot resume at a command nested inside it. As with `.ad` replay, restore any state and environment values the skipped steps would have set before you resume.

## Export `.ad` scripts to Maestro YAML

To run a recorded flow with Maestro, export the `.ad` script to Maestro YAML:

```bash
agent-device replay export ./workflows/checkout.ad --out ./maestro/checkout.yaml
```

`replay export` only converts the file: it does not start the daemon or contact a device. Without `--out`, it prints the YAML to stdout.

Each `open <appId>` exports with an explicit `launchApp.appId`, so a flow can switch between apps and return to the original app. The first app remains the flow’s default `appId`; relaunch options and app-specific deep links stay attached to their authored targets.

Deep links, including schemes without `//` such as `tel:` and `mailto:`, export as `openLink`. A standalone `open tel:+15551234567` emits only the link command; `open com.example.app mailto:agent@example.test` emits the app launch followed by the link.

On the native iOS runner, use `tapOn` on a visible dismissal control. If the app supports drag dismissal, use a `swipe` that stays above the keyboard.

Export is strict. It writes Maestro YAML for compatible flow actions such as app launch, taps, long press, text input, keyboard dismiss/enter, back, home, text visibility assertions, coordinate swipes, basic scroll, screenshots, and `.ad` `env` directives. `home` exports as `pressKey: Home`, so flows that visit the home screen and reopen the app can be exported. Agent-only inspection or maintenance actions such as `snapshot`, `get`, `record`, `trace`, `settings`, and unsupported selector shapes fail with the source line and action instead of being silently dropped. Known semantic differences are reported as warnings; for example, `.ad` `fill` exports as `tapOn` plus `inputText`, which may append text in Maestro rather than replacing existing field contents. Native `.ad` `label=` selectors export as Maestro `text:` selectors and warn because Maestro text matching is broader than label-only matching. A strict `wait absent` is reported as unsupported rather than mapped to Maestro’s more lenient `notVisible` condition.

## Troubleshooting

* A flow fails on unsupported syntax:
  * Check [ADR 0015](https://github.com/callstack/agent-device/blob/main/docs/adr/0015-direct-maestro-engine.md). If the missing feature matters to your suite, open a focused issue with a small flow snippet.

# Security and trust

> Security and trust guidance for agent-device local app automation, device permissions, screenshots, recordings, logs, network dumps, audio probes, traces, and reports.

`agent-device` runs locally by default and can control every device, simulator, emulator, and desktop app your user account can reach. Treat it like any developer tool that interacts with apps, captures screens, and reads diagnostic output.

## Local control

* Device automation runs through the installed CLI and platform tooling such as Xcode, ADB, Amazon Vega CLI/VDA, macOS accessibility APIs, and Linux AT-SPI.
* The MCP server exposes structured tools for `agent-device` commands. Local-only workflows stay CLI-only. The MCP server never exposes generic shell execution.
* Run mutating commands serially against one session. For parallel work, use separate sessions and devices.

## Daemon trust model

CLI commands run through a per-user background daemon:

* The daemon binds to `127.0.0.1` only, on ephemeral ports, for both its socket and HTTP transports. It is not reachable from the network unless you put your own proxy in front of it.
* Command (RPC), upload, artifact-download, and `/admin/human-control/*` requests must present a token that the daemon generates fresh on each start (24 random bytes). The only unauthenticated endpoint is `GET /health`, which returns only liveness, package and protocol version, instance ID, and host CPU architecture; like the rest of the server, it is reachable only over loopback. The token is stored in `daemon.json` inside the daemon state directory (`~/.agent-device` for packaged installs; source checkouts use a worktree-scoped directory under `~/.agent-device/dev/`) with `0600` permissions. Anyone who can read that file already has your user account.
* A client reuses a running daemon only when the daemon runs the same version and the same code. Two installs of the same published version share one daemon. An older client refuses to replace a reachable daemon on a newer version, so it does not disrupt that daemon’s sessions; upgrade the client instead. Any other mismatch, such as a source checkout against an install, restarts the daemon instead of running code the client cannot identify. The code check compares file sizes and timestamps, not contents, so it does not detect an install whose files were hand-replaced under the same version.
* Artifact uploads are size-capped, filenames are sanitized, and archive extraction rejects path-traversal entries. Artifact downloads resolve through server-side IDs, never client-supplied paths.
* `install-from-source` protects the daemon host while it downloads and extracts the artifact; it does not vouch for the app inside. An app installed and launched on an iOS simulator runs as a process on the host Mac, so treat permission to send install requests as permission to run code on that Mac.

For remote or cloud deployments, you can add a custom auth hook for remotely consumable HTTP routes: set `AGENT_DEVICE_HTTP_AUTH_HOOK` to a module path that the daemon imports, and `AGENT_DEVICE_HTTP_AUTH_EXPORT` to select the export. Relative hook paths resolve from the daemon host’s working directory. The host-local `/admin/human-control/*` route uses the daemon token instead.
