The hook runs with the daemon’s full privileges, so treat it as trusted code: point it only at a read-only path you control, never at a location that less-trusted users or processes can write to. Whoever controls the daemon’s environment controls the hook. On the upload routes, the hook context carries a `signal` that aborts when the upload request times out or its client disconnects. The daemon stops waiting for the hook at that point, so a hook that calls a slow identity service can use the signal to stop that call.

Lease-owner human-control RPCs pass normal authentication and tenant/lease admission. They can target only the admitted lease’s device and cannot alter a host administrator’s hold. Host administration is a separate capability: the daemon accepts `/admin/human-control/*` only on its loopback listener with the local daemon token, and `agent-device proxy` does not forward `/admin/*`. Holds and leases live in memory; neither survives a daemon restart.

When a hook is configured, it must attest a `tenantId` on every request it wants admitted. If the hook’s result has no `tenantId`, the daemon rejects the request with 401. It never falls back to a tenant the client declares (RPC body `meta.tenantId` or `flags.tenant`, or the `x-agent-device-tenant` header on the upload, artifact-download, and diagnostics routes), and it never admits the request unscoped. This keeps a caller with a shared token from claiming another tenant’s identity, or from reading a tenant-owned session or artifact by declaring no tenant. Deployments without a hook are unaffected.

## Apple runner

Apple targets (iOS, tvOS, visionOS, and macOS) are driven through an XCTest runner that listens on its own port, separate from the daemon:

* On simulators and macOS, the runner binds to `127.0.0.1` only.
* On a physical device, the runner listens on the device’s network interfaces, because a device connected over Wi-Fi is reached through its CoreDevice network tunnel. A cabled device is reached over USB. The runner closes any connection that arrives on another network interface, such as another machine on the same Wi-Fi, before reading it.
* Every request must present a token that the daemon generates fresh for each runner launch (24 random bytes). The runner refuses to start without one, and rejects a request that lacks it before decoding the request body. The token reaches the runner through its launch configuration, never a command line, and the app under test does not receive it. On the host it is stored in owner-only (`0600`) files: the runner lease, the per-session `.xctestrun` and its `.json` sibling, and, for simulators, the XCTest session log Xcode writes. A simulator runner is a process on your Mac, so the token is also in its environment, which only your user account and root can read.
* A runner built by an earlier agent-device version does not require the token. agent-device stops it before sending it any command that changes the device. A configured `iosXctestrunFile` must be built by the same agent-device version.

## Sensitive artifacts

Screenshots, recordings, traces, logs, network dumps, audio probes, replay files, provider-hosted cloud videos and logs, and reports can contain private UI state, credentials, tokens, request data, timing signals, or customer information. Store them in a controlled directory, review them before sharing, and don’t commit them unless they are deliberately sanitized fixtures.

Cloud provider artifact URLs returned by `artifacts`, `close --json`, or `disconnect --json` may be provider dashboard URLs, public share links, or pre-signed download URLs. Treat the URLs themselves as credentials until you know the provider’s sharing and expiry policy.

The privacy controls for typed input (`fill --text-stdin` and `--record-as`) keep the literal out of agent-device’s own responses, diagnostics, and recorded scripts. They do not rewrite what the platform records: on iOS, XCTest writes its own diagnostic logs and its `.xcresult` bundle under the Apple runner’s derived directory, and typed text can appear in both, on a simulator or a physical device. Treat those as sensitive, and use test-only credentials when they may be kept or shared.

## Permissions

Some targets require local permissions or developer setup:

* iOS, tvOS, and macOS automation uses Xcode tooling; physical devices may require signing or Developer Mode.
* Android automation uses ADB and requires a trusted emulator or device connection.
* Vega OS automation uses Vega CLI/VDA with the local Vega Virtual Device only; `agent-device` does not control physical devices that run Vega OS. Fire TV devices that run Fire OS are Android-based and automate over ADB as Android TV devices.
* macOS desktop automation requires Accessibility permission, and screen capture workflows may require Screen Recording permission.

## Network and updates

Interactive CLI runs may check npm for newer `agent-device` releases and print an upgrade suggestion. Set `AGENT_DEVICE_NO_UPDATE_NOTIFIER=1` to turn off the notice.

Network inspection commands collect only the traffic that the active app or session tooling can see. Review network artifacts before sharing, because headers and payloads can contain secrets.

## Report a vulnerability

Report security issues privately to Callstack at <hello@callstack.com>. Do not open a public issue for a vulnerability that exposes user data, credentials, device access, or remote execution risk.

# Selectors

Target an element by what it says or is, instead of a snapshot ref. Use `find` to search by text, label, value, role, or id, or pass a selector expression to any command that takes a target.

```bash
agent-device find "Settings" click
agent-device find text "Sign In" click
agent-device find label "Email" fill "user@example.com"
agent-device find value "Search" click
agent-device type "query"
agent-device find role button click
agent-device find id "com.example:id/login" click
agent-device find "Follow" list
```

## Find an element

`find <query> [action]` and `find <locator> <query> [action] [value]` take an optional locator (`text`, `label`, `value`, `role`, or `id`), the query, and an optional action; the action defaults to `click`. Without a locator it searches labels, values, and ids. Text matches ignore case, and a field containing the query matches too; an exact match wins over a partial one.

Actions:

* `click` (default; `press` and `tap` are aliases)
* `list`
* `focus`
* `fill <text>`
* `type <text>`
* `exists`
* `wait [timeoutMs]`
* `get text`, `get attrs`

`list` is read-only: it returns every match with its `@ref` and never taps, so use it to inspect matches before you act. `find` has no `longpress` or `swipe` action; run `list`, then run the gesture on the ref you picked, for example `longpress @e14`.

When more than one element matches, the mutating actions (`click`, `focus`, `fill`, `type`) reject the query and list the candidates. This applies to text queries and selector expressions alike. Read-only actions (`exists`, `wait`, `get`) use the first match, and `list` returns every match. Add `--first` or `--last` to pick a match by position instead.

```bash
agent-device find "Follow" click --first
```

A read-only `find` that prints a ref (`get text`, `get attrs`, `list`) publishes only the refs it returns, so it ends the earlier snapshot’s refs. A later `get` or `wait` on one of those older refs fails with `error.details.reason: ref_not_issued` instead of reading whichever element now has that number. Use a ref the `find` printed, or run `snapshot -i` again.

Tips:

* `find role <value>` and the `role=` selector key use the same role names that snapshots show. See [Structured node fields](/docs/snapshots#structured-node-fields---json).

* Use `find ... wait <timeoutMs>` to wait for an element to appear.

* Pair `find` with a scoped snapshot (`snapshot -s "<label>"`) for speed.

* \[Android] If the matched node is not hittable, agent-device clicks or focuses the nearest hittable ancestor.

* `find ... focus` and `find ... type` aim at a text field. If the match is a field or sits inside one, that field is the target, even when it is not hittable or has other fields beside it. Otherwise the target is the one enabled on-screen field inside the match.

  * Several enabled on-screen fields inside the match refuse with `AMBIGUOUS_MATCH` and the field candidates.
  * A disabled target refuses with `COMMAND_FAILED` and reason `target_disabled`. This includes a match whose only on-screen fields are disabled.
  * A match or field covered by another visible element refuses with `COMMAND_FAILED` and reason `target_covered`.
  * A target outside the screen refuses with `COMMAND_FAILED` and reason `offscreen_ref`, as `click @ref` does. `find` prefers an on-screen match, so this happens only when the chosen target is off screen.
  * A target that still reports `hittable: false` is focused, and the response adds `targetHittable: false` and a `hint`, as `press`, `click`, and `fill` do.
  * Web text boxes are not recognized as text fields, so a web match keeps its own aim.

* Use `fill` to find a field and replace its text in one step. To append to the text in the focused field, use `click` or `press`, then `type`.

## Selector syntax

A selector expression is one or more `key=value` terms separated by spaces. An element must match every term. Commands that take a target, such as `press`, `fill`, `longpress`, `get`, `is`, `wait`, and `scroll --until`, accept a selector wherever they accept an `@ref`. `find` accepts one as its query. `agent-device help selectors` prints this syntax.

```bash
agent-device press 'role=button label="Continue"'
agent-device fill 'label="Email" editable=true' "qa@example.com"
agent-device wait 'id="checkout-total"' 5000
agent-device press 'id="submit" || label="Submit order"'
agent-device find 'role=button label="Follow"' list
```

Text keys:

| Key           | Matches                                                                             |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `id`          | The element’s identifier (test ID, resource ID, accessibility identifier)           |
| `label`       | The accessibility label                                                             |
| `value`       | The accessibility value                                                             |
| `text`        | The first non-empty of label, value, and identifier                                 |
| `role`        | The role shown in brackets in snapshot output (`button`, `text-field`, `switch`, …) |
| `appname`     | The owning app’s name, on desktop targets that report it                            |
| `windowtitle` | The owning window’s title, on desktop targets that report it                        |

Text values match the whole field, ignoring case and extra whitespace: `label="sign in"` matches `Sign In` but not `Sign In Now`. For partial matches, use `find`.

On Android, `id=` matches the element’s full resource-id, which keeps its `pkg:id/name` form for native XML ids, while a React Native `testID` arrives bare (`id="login"`). A Jetpack Compose `Modifier.testTag` is exposed to agent-device only when the app sets `semantics { testTagsAsResourceId = true }`; then `id="<tag>"` matches it.

Boolean keys: `visible`, `hidden`, `editable`, `selected`, `checked`, `focused`, `enabled`, `hittable`. Write `visible=true` or `visible=false`; a bare `visible` means `visible=true`.

`checked` (and `is checked`) reads the state of a checkable control (switch, checkbox, radio). `checked=true` matches only an explicitly checked control and `checked=false` only an explicitly unchecked one; an iOS `mixed` state and a control with no checked state match neither.

`editable` (and `is editable`) uses the node’s native `editable` fact when the snapshot carries one, so a custom text view can match and a read-only field cannot. Without the fact it is inferred from the element type. A disabled element is never editable.

Quoting and alternatives:

* Quote values that contain spaces, with double or single quotes: `label="Sign in"`. Escape a quote inside a value with a backslash: `label="Say \"hi\""`.
* Wrap the whole expression in single quotes in the shell so it reaches agent-device as one argument.
* Separate alternatives with `||`. agent-device tries them left to right and uses the first one that resolves.
* Keys are case-insensitive. Commands that take a target reject an unknown key, such as `button="Save"`; write `role=button label="Save"` instead.

## Response shape (click)

`find "<query>" click --json` returns metadata for the element it matched, taken from the resolved snapshot node:

```json
{
  "ref": "@e3",
  "locator": "any",
  "query": "Sign In",
  "x": 195,
  "y": 422
}
```

* `ref` — snapshot ref of the matched (or nearest hittable ancestor) element.
* `locator` — the locator used (`any`, `text`, `label`, `value`, `role`, `id`).
* `query` — the search term as provided.
* `x`, `y` — tap coordinates derived from the matched element’s rect center.

# Sessions

A session ties your commands to one device and app, so state and snapshots carry over from one command to the next.

```bash
agent-device open Settings --platform ios
agent-device session list
agent-device open Contacts          # change app in this workspace's session
agent-device close
```

You don’t need to name a session. The implicit session is scoped to your git worktree (or current working directory) and to the platform the command selects: `--platform ios` runs in the `ios` session and `--platform android` in the `android` session. A session opened without `--platform` uses the platform-less `default` session, and commands that name a platform still join it as long as they match its device. Agents in different worktrees do not attach to each other’s implicit session; a named session (`--session <name>`) is shared across worktrees. Implicit web sessions in different worktrees also use separate browsers, so they can run at the same time.

## Find a session’s logs and artifacts

When a session starts, human output prints a `Session state: <path>` line and JSON output includes `sessionStateDir`. That directory holds the session’s artifacts; inspect or delete it after the run. JSON output also includes `runnerLogPath` and `requestLogPath` when available.

Each session artifact directory contains:

* `requests/<request-id>.ndjson` - daemon request diagnostics for this session.
* `events.ndjson` - session event timeline for requests and recorded actions; rotates to `events.ndjson.1` before an entry would exceed 5 MiB (`AGENT_DEVICE_EVENT_LOG_MAX_BYTES`, whole bytes), with `events.ndjson.window.json` tracking the retained files so `events` cursors within the retained window stay valid across rotation. Older cursors expire.
* `runner.log` - Apple runner and `xcodebuild` build/start output for this session.
* `app.log` - app/device logs when `logs start` or `logs clear --restart` is active.

`events.ndjson` leaves out user-entered content. It keeps command names, status, durations, bounded device/app inventory previews, lifecycle outcomes, artifact basenames, and structural action details such as scroll distance/direction, safe refs, and coordinates. User-entered text, clipboard contents, push/event payloads, selector values, free-form flags/messages/paths, and raw unknown command arguments are omitted or replaced with content-free placeholders. `--no-record` suppresses recorded action entries; request start/finish entries still record command, status, and timing.

The timeline is best effort. An event line larger than the configured file cap or 16 MiB is dropped. The per-session limit is 128 events and 16 MiB of event data, including the write in progress. Further events are dropped until capacity is available. These drops do not fail the command, and failed entries are not replayed. To capture write or rotation failure diagnostics while reproducing missing entries, run the command with `--debug`, then look for `session_event_log_write_failed` in `requests/<request-id>.ndjson` inside the session artifact directory. An active `trace` also records these diagnostics in its trace file.

To debug a specific run, start with the session artifact directory. The top-level daemon log only covers daemon startup and lifecycle issues.

## Share a session by name

Name a session only when you want a shared, reusable handle. Pass `--session <name>` or set `AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION`:

```bash
agent-device open Contacts --platform ios --session my-session
agent-device snapshot -i
agent-device close --session my-session
```

Don’t run commands that change state in parallel on the same session. Run actions such as `open`, `press`, `fill`, `type`, `scroll`, `back`, `alert`, `replay`, `batch`, and `close` one at a time.

## Lock a named session to a device

A lock keeps a named session’s commands on its device: per-call selectors that conflict with the session are rejected or dropped. Most local automation doesn’t need one, because implicit sessions are already scoped to the workspace.

Setting `AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION` turns on the lock in `reject` mode by default. Choose how conflicts are handled with `--session-lock reject|strip`, `AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION_LOCK=reject|strip`, or the `sessionLock` config key:

```bash
AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION=qa-ios AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION_LOCK=strip agent-device snapshot --platform android
```

The MCP server and the AI SDK tools apply the same lock. They read `AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION`, `AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION_LOCK`, `AGENT_DEVICE_PLATFORM`, and the `sessionLock` config key from the process that serves the tools. A session or platform named in a tool call does not turn on the lock.

* `reject` fails a command whose selectors conflict with the lock.
* `strip` drops conflicting platform and scope selectors (`--platform`, `--target`, `--ios-simulator-device-set`, `--android-device-allowlist`) and runs the command on the locked device. Only those selectors are dropped.
* In either mode, a selector that names a different device than the lock (`--udid`, `--serial`, `--device`) is never dropped. The command fails with `INVALID_ARGS` and names both the requested and the locked device, because continuing would run it on a device you did not select. If you want the requested device, close the locked session; if you want the locked one, remove the selector.
* CLI scope flags normally override environment values. With `strip` active, conflicting per-call selectors are ignored instead.
* The daemon enforces the lock, so CLI, Node.js client, and direct RPC requests get the same conflict handling. Direct RPC callers pass `meta.lockPolicy` and optional `meta.lockPlatform` on `agent_device.command` requests.
* `batch` steps keep the batch’s `--platform` under a lock; see [Batching](/docs/batching).

## Drive two platforms from one checkout

You don’t need to name sessions: `--platform` selects that platform’s implicit session, so each platform keeps its own device, app, and artifact directory.

```bash
agent-device open Demo --platform ios
agent-device open Demo --platform android   # its own session, not a conflict with the iOS one
agent-device snapshot --platform android
agent-device close --platform ios
```

Once a workspace holds more than one implicit session, a command that names neither `--platform` nor `--session` fails with `AMBIGUOUS_MATCH` instead of guessing which device to drive. That includes `close`, so add `--platform` (or `--session <address>`) to each teardown line too. `session list`, `devices`, `doctor`, `capabilities`, and `apps` don’t claim a session, so they still work; `session list` prints the `address` that `--session` accepts.

## Shut down the device on close

Add `--shutdown` to shut down an Apple simulator or Android emulator when you close the session. Use it in CI and on shared hosts so devices don’t keep running after the run:

```bash
agent-device close --shutdown
```

Without `--shutdown`, `close` can keep a ready, idle iOS simulator runner warm for the next `open` when its listener connection is still live and the session has no screen recording or device lease. Unfinished runner startup is stopped. If you shut that simulator down yourself while the runner is retained, losing its listener connection stops the retained runner. Idle retained runners also stop when their daemon shuts down gracefully.

## Wait for a slow or busy device

A never-booted iOS Simulator can take several minutes to finish its first boot. Give `open` (or `prepare ios-runner`) a `--timeout` long enough to cover it. The session claims the device from the first `open` onward, so another workspace gets `DEVICE_IN_USE` the whole time:

```bash
agent-device open Settings --platform ios --udid <udid> --timeout 600000
```

Without `--timeout`, the command gives up after about 90 seconds, often before a first boot finishes. When the budget runs out, the command fails with `error.details.reason: boot_timeout`, but the Simulator or emulator keeps booting, so a retry finds it further along.

When another session holds the device but will release it soon — a parallel agent finishing its run — `open --wait <ms>` waits for the device instead of failing at once, and reports who holds it while it waits:

```bash
agent-device open Demo --platform android --wait 60000
```

If the wait runs out while the device is still busy, `open` fails with `DEVICE_IN_USE` and names the session address that holds it; `close --session <address>` releases it. Each waiting `open` gets its full wait: if another waiter gets the device first, the rest keep waiting for what is left of their own budget, so several agents can queue on one device.

`--wait` waits only for another session. A device claimed by another workspace’s daemon is never waited for; `open` fails at once and names the command that releases it. Device-mutating commands like `install` and `reinstall` don’t wait either: while a session other than yours holds the device, they fail at once with `DEVICE_IN_USE`. Copying the owner’s `--session` address doesn’t change that — the claim must also record your workspace, so a command run from another checkout is refused even under the owner’s name. The error names the owner when the claim is readable; when it isn’t, `agent-device device status` shows what holds the device.

## Release a device another session or workspace holds

Each daemon claims the devices its sessions use. A claim whose owner is live, or can’t be proven gone, blocks `open` from another workspace, and blocks device-mutating commands like `install` from any other owner — another session, or the same session name from another workspace. List the claims on this host without starting a daemon:

```bash
agent-device device status
agent-device device status --platform ios --udid <udid>
agent-device device status --stale
```

Normal output shows live claims and claims that need attention, then counts the stale claims it hides in one line; `--stale` lists those. A stale claim’s owner process exited, its PID now belongs to another process, its state directory was deleted, or a newer daemon replaced it. In the last two cases the owner process can still be running, so inspect each one before you act. Scope either view with `--platform` plus `--udid` (Apple) or `--serial` (Android).

`--json` reports each claimed device once as `acquirable`, an inspection of whether a new session can take it now. It cannot see a reboot and runs no recovery, so `open` may decide differently. `blockedBy` names why not, and `owner` identifies the claim’s owner when its record decodes: the holder that blocks the device or, on an acquirable device, the reclaimable dead owner `open` would settle. A daemon’s own abandoned claim is reported as blocked by that live owner, but `open` through that same daemon may still take it. A stale claim whose owner is provably gone and retains no resource does not block by itself. `hiddenStaleClaims` counts the claim records this view hides and is not an availability signal, so read `acquirable`: a hidden owner whose PID was reused or whose state directory is gone, and pending resource cleanup, each still block the device.

To free a device:

* If the owner is still running, close its session from its own workspace, or stop its daemon with `agent-device daemon stop --state-dir <owner state dir>`.
* If the owner provably can’t release the claim, because its process exited or a newer daemon replaced it, run `agent-device device release --stale`. It settles the durable resources that owner left behind, then clears the claim; if those resources don’t settle, the claim stays. Live, uncertain, PID-reused, corrupt, and deleted-state-directory claims are refused with the reason; `device release` never forces them.
* `open` replaces such a claim itself once that owner’s durable resources are settled.
* If the device rebooted after a live owner’s claim was taken, the reboot already ended that owner’s app, runner, and accessibility session. `open` settles the owner’s durable resources, takes the claim, and reports the release in `warnings`. `device release --stale` never checks for a reboot, so it keeps refusing a claim whose owner is live.

## Hold a device while an external command runs

Tools like `xcrun simctl install` or `expo run:ios` install without going through a session, so they ignore claims. To keep other sessions off the device while one runs, claim it first with an app-less `open` on a uniquely named session, and run the command only if the claim succeeds:

```bash
udid=<udid>
claim="build-$$"
agent-device open --platform ios --udid "$udid" --session "$claim" --timeout 600000 || exit
trap 'agent-device close --session "$claim"' EXIT
xcrun simctl install "$udid" ./App.app
```

* `|| exit` stops the script when another session holds the device (`DEVICE_IN_USE`), so the command never runs unfenced. Add `--wait <ms>` to `open` to queue for the device instead.
* The script exits with the command’s status, as long as the command is the last line. To run more after it, save `status=$?` and finish with `exit "$status"`.
* The `trap` closes the session whether the command succeeds or fails. Add `--shutdown` to `close` to shut the simulator or emulator down afterwards.
* `open` without an app boots the device if needed and claims it, so the first call on a cold simulator can take minutes.
* This is a session claim, not a claim owned by your process. If the shell dies without running its `trap` (for example `kill -9`), the session keeps the device until you run `agent-device close --session <name>`. Find the name with `agent-device session list`. The tool itself is not stopped from touching the device; only other agent-device sessions are fenced off.

## Notes

* `open <app>` in an existing session switches the active app and updates the session’s bundle id. On iOS, to see whether the session app held the foreground during a command, read the [`targetActivation` disclosure](/docs/commands#foreground-repairs-on-ios).
* For remote `connect --remote-config` sessions, see [Commands](/docs/commands#remote-metro-workflow).

For replay scripts and deterministic E2E guidance, see [Replay and E2E testing](/docs/replay-e2e).

# Snapshots

Take a snapshot to read the UI as a structured tree and get refs (`@e1`, `@e2`, …) for the elements on the current screen.

```bash
agent-device snapshot                    # Full accessibility tree
agent-device snapshot -i                 # Interactive elements only (recommended)
agent-device snapshot -d 3               # Limit depth to 3 levels
agent-device snapshot -s "Contacts"      # Scope to label/identifier
agent-device snapshot -i -d 5            # Combine options
agent-device snapshot --actions          # Name custom actions merged into elements (iOS simulator)
agent-device diff snapshot               # Structural diff vs previous session baseline
```

| Option           | Description                                                                                             |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--diff`         | Structural diff against the previous session baseline (alias for `diff snapshot`)                       |
| `-i`             | Interactive-only output                                                                                 |
| `-d <depth>`     | Limit tree depth                                                                                        |
| `-s <scope>`     | Scope to label, value, identifier, or `@ref` ([Scope a snapshot](#scope-a-snapshot))                    |
| `--raw`          | Full provider tree instead of the visible-first agent view                                              |
| `--actions`      | Name the custom accessibility actions merged inside an element (iOS simulator)                          |
| `--observe-only` | Read the session app without activating it or repairing foreground (local iOS and iPadOS sessions only) |
| `--force-full`   | Re-emit the full tree even when it is unchanged since the previous snapshot                             |
| `--timeout <ms>` | Maximum wall-clock time for the snapshot command                                                        |

`--actions` limits:

* Works on iOS simulators only. Physical iOS devices, macOS, and Android targets reject the flag.
* It names the affordances an element merged away (iOS `UIAccessibilityCustomAction`, React Native `accessibilityActions`), so a card whose reply/options controls are not separate elements still lists them.
* You can read the names but not trigger them. To use an affordance, go through the element’s detail screen, find the same control exposed as a labeled element elsewhere, or tap by coordinates from its rect.
* Each merged element costs one accessibility round trip, so the pass is opt-in and capped. When it cannot read every candidate, the response says how many it read. A missing list on an unread element does not mean the element has no actions.
* You can’t combine it with `--raw`. The CLI, the Node client, and MCP all reject the pair with `INVALID_ARGS` before touching the device.

## iOS observe-only snapshots

`agent-device snapshot --observe-only` reads the bound iOS or iPadOS app without activating it or repairing its foreground state. An ordinary snapshot brings a backgrounded session app back and discloses that with `targetActivation`; an observe-only snapshot refuses instead, so the screen is left exactly as it was. Other platforms, provider-owned sessions, and `--diff` are unsupported.

The runner refuses with `OBSERVATION_UNAVAILABLE` (also named by `details.runnerErrorCode`) unless the app reports `runningForeground` before and after the capture under one process identity. It does not substitute SpringBoard or a presented system surface, and it refuses the same way when it can read a system alert over the app. A success does not prove that no alert is present: an alert the runner cannot read leaves the app tree as the answer. The host refuses with `COMMAND_FAILED` and `details.reason: "observation-unavailable"` when a runner answers an observe-only request without `observation` or with a `targetActivation` fact. Successful JSON includes:

```json
{
  "observation": {
    "mode": "observe-only",
    "activationPerformed": false,
    "appState": "runningForeground",
    "appStateSource": "xcuiapplication-state"
  }
}
```

This reports **XCUIApplication state, not verified foreground ownership**: XCTest can report that state incorrectly when another app owns the screen ([#2696](https://github.com/callstack/agent-device/issues/2696)). Observe-only results never carry `targetActivation`. Regular snapshots retain their existing repair and disclosure behavior ([#2682](https://github.com/callstack/agent-device/issues/2682), [#2694](https://github.com/callstack/agent-device/issues/2694)).

## Keep snapshots small and current

* iOS and Android produce the same kind of snapshot: visible elements first, refs you can act on now, and hints that point to hidden list content.
* Use `snapshot -i` by default in agent loops.
* On tvOS, regular snapshots can mark the outer tile as focused when duplicate accessibility wrappers collapse. Use `snapshot --raw` to see which wrapper the app reports as focused.
* On Android, `snapshot -i` also keeps the title and message of a standard alert dialog, so you can see what its buttons confirm.
* When the Android snapshot helper captures the tree, the `Page:` and `App:` lines (`appName` and `appBundleId` in `--json`) name the foreground application window: active or focused, at the highest layer, and not a system UI or keyboard window. After a failed `open`, for example, they name the launcher. An app other than the session app shows its package name in both lines. `androidSnapshot.foregroundWindowPackage` in `--json` carries it, and the session keeps its app. The UIAutomator fallback names the session app.
* On Android, repeating an unfiltered snapshot when nothing on screen changed (content or bounds) returns a short acknowledgement instead of the tree. `-i`, `-d`, `-s`, `--json`, and `--raw` always print full output. Add `--force-full` to get the full tree anyway.
* The default text output is a compact view for planning and targeting actions. It lists visible elements first and may collapse helper and accessibility noise. Use `--raw` or `--json` when you need the full provider tree. Keep `--raw` for troubleshooting, such as when you need the full off-screen tree that summaries abbreviate.
* Off-screen interactive content is collapsed into summaries that show only a few labels, such as `[off-screen below] 3 interactive items: "Privacy", "Battery", "About"`.
* If your target only appears in an off-screen summary, run `scroll <direction> --until <selector>` to stop on it, or `scroll <direction> --settle` to get the diff with fresh refs. See [Interactions](/docs/commands#interactions).
* When agent-device knows which container holds the hidden content, it shows the summary inside that scroll or list container, for example `[content above scroll-area hidden]` or `[content below list hidden]`.
* In a regular (non-`--raw`) snapshot, a listed element whose frame has no area is marked `[unmeasured]`: nothing confirms it is on screen. On iOS, a Flutter scroll view keeps its scrolled-out content this way. If the element is inside scrollable content, run `scroll <direction> --until <selector>` before acting on it.
* Add `-s "<label>"` (or `-s @ref`) to limit output to one part of the screen. See [Scope a snapshot](#scope-a-snapshot).
* Add `-d <depth>` when you only need the upper layers of the hierarchy.
* If `snapshot -i -d <n>` reports no interactive elements at that depth, retry once without `-d` instead of taking more shallow snapshots.
* Take a new snapshot after any UI change before you reuse refs.
* On Android, right after navigation or a submit, snapshot capture retries trees that look stale for a short time, and `@ref` interactions refresh during that window. If `snapshot -i` still disagrees with the screen, trust `screenshot`, wait briefly, and take one fresh snapshot instead of looping on stale ones.
* If Android animations make runs flaky, run `settings animations off` before the run and `settings animations on` after it.
* On a device cloud, the provider’s driver reads the tree. A screen that never goes still — a looping video, a live ticker, continuous animation — can make that read run out of time while `screenshot` still works. When the request is cancelled, agent-device stops waiting for the read, but the daemon and session stay alive, and the provider may keep reading and hold up that session’s queue. A larger `--timeout` does not extend the read, and `settings animations` is not available on hosted WebDriver sessions.
* Run `diff snapshot` between UI changes to check what changed with less output. The first run records a baseline (`baselineInitialized: true` in JSON). Later runs print unified-style lines (`+` added, `-` removed, unchanged context) and update the baseline after each call.

## Example output

```bash
agent-device snapshot -i
# Output:
# Snapshot: 9 visible nodes (14 total)
# @e1 [application] "Contacts"
#   @e2 [window]
#     @e3 [other]
#   @e4 [other] "Lists"
#     @e5 [navigation-bar] "Lists"
#       @e6 [button] "Lists"
#       @e7 [text] "Contacts"
#     @e8 [other] "John Doe"
#       @e9 [other] "John Doe"
# [off-screen below] 2 interactive items: "All Contacts", "New List"
```

With Android Appium, `snapshot --json` includes `viewport: { "width": …, "height": … }` when the driver can measure the display. These dimensions use the same coordinates as node rectangles and are refreshed for each capture, including after rotation. Opening the keyboard can shrink the app’s content without shrinking the display viewport. An empty or sparse tree can still have a viewport; when the measurements disagree or either measurement is unavailable, `viewport` is absent.

## Structured node fields (`--json`)

Every node in `snapshot --json` output carries `kind`, next to `type` when the platform reports one:

* `type` is the raw platform class, verbatim: `Button` / `StaticText` from XCUI, `android.widget.Button` from the Android hierarchy. It differs by platform for the same UI role.
* `kind` is the platform-neutral role shown in brackets in text output (`button`, `text-field`, `text`, `switch`, `link`, …). It is the same on every platform and backend, in both `snapshot` and `snapshot -i`, so text and JSON output always agree on a node’s role.

```json
{ "ref": "e4", "type": "android.widget.Button", "kind": "button", "label": "Send code" }
{ "ref": "e40", "type": "Button", "role": "UIButton", "kind": "button", "label": "Continue to catalog" }
```

On iOS, `role` (when present) is the native AX class (`UIButton`), carried only on iOS nodes. `kind` is the cross-platform role, present on every node on every platform.

A node the occlusion scan finds covered carries `interactionBlocked: "covered"`, and when the scan can name what draws on top of it, `coveredBy` beside it: the cover’s `kind`, its accessible `label` when it has one, and its `rect`:

```json
{
  "ref": "e10",
  "kind": "text",
  "label": "Session health",
  "interactionBlocked": "covered",
  "coveredBy": {
    "kind": "group",
    "label": "Confirm catalog refresh",
    "rect": { "x": 41, "y": 327, "width": 320, "height": 248 }
  }
}
```

A persistent bar publishes `persistentBar: true`. Its `coveredBy.kind` is `tab-bar`, `toolbar`, `navigation-bar`, or `bottom-navigation`. The cover can be identified by its type, role, or subrole. Other covers use their presented role. For example, an alert’s container may publish as `group` with the alert’s accessible name. When a scroll container of the covered node reports hidden content toward the bar and its frame reaches beyond the bar on the bar-free side, the bar also publishes `scrollCanReveal: true`: a scroll can reveal the node clear of the bar.

A `click`/`press`/`fill`/`find ... focus` refused on that node repeats the same description in `error.details.coveredBy` and names it in `error.hint`. For a persistent bar, use a different visible target or inspect with a snapshot or screenshot before retrying. Audit reports covered controls inside scroll containers, except a control or row under a persistent bar marked `scrollCanReveal`. `coveredBy` is diagnostic and has no ref, so the cover is not an actionable target. It is absent when nothing nameable covers — an anonymous container with no accessible name that is not a persistent bar, or a backend policy that reports only the boolean, such as an Android replacement surface — and those refusals say only that the target is covered.

`role=` selectors (and `find role=...`) match the `kind` vocabulary: a node whose `kind` is `text` or `text-field` always matches `role=text` / `role=text-field`, the bracketed word a snapshot shows for that node. The raw leaf classes — `role=statictext`, `role=edittext`, `role=textview`, `role=searchfield`, and the rest of the leaf vocabulary — also match as deprecated aliases, each only on nodes that carried that class (so `role=linearlayout` never matches a `FrameLayout` row the way a shared `group` alias would). Use the `kind` spelling in your selectors.

## Scope a snapshot

```bash
agent-device snapshot -i -s "Shipping address"
agent-device snapshot -s @e12
```

* `-s <text>` returns the subtree of the first node, in document order, whose label, value, or identifier contains the text (case-insensitive) and whose subtree still has content in the view you asked for. That node becomes the new root at depth 0.
* With `-i`, scoping to a layout container returns the actionable elements inside it, even when the container itself is filtered out.
* `-d` counts from the scope root.
* `-s @ref` scopes by that element’s label from the last snapshot.
* When nothing matches, you get an empty snapshot, not the full tree.

## Truncated captures

`truncated: true` means the Android snapshot helper or the iOS Simulator accessibility bridge hit its 5000-node limit, or the web provider hit its own bound. On Android the limit applies before any `-s` scope. The Apple runner does not return a partial tree: above its limit (50,000 nodes, or 5,000 with `--raw`) the snapshot fails with a hint to scope it or take a screenshot instead.

Every backend walks the tree in document order, so what gets cut is what comes last: footers, tab bars, items after a long list, even when they are on screen. The snapshot carries a warning when this happens. Navigate or scroll so fewer elements render and snapshot again, and use `screenshot` as the visual truth for the rest.

## Coordinates and viewport

`viewport: { width, height }` names the box the node rects are measured in. It uses the same coordinate space and orientation as the rects, so you can scale and clip against the screen the snapshot was taken on instead of guessing it from the largest rect.

* iOS reports the app window, so iPad Split View and a foldable panel do not inflate it.
* Android and Apple TV report the measured screen. Android reports it under `--raw` too, since the raw rects are measured on the same screen.
* The Tizen and webOS TV plugins report the page’s layout viewport in CSS pixels, which is not the screenshot size: a webOS app at 1280x720 fills only the top-left 1280x720 of a 1920x1080 capture.
* It is absent when the capture measured no box: a macOS capture, whose rects are absolute in window space; a web or Linux capture, which reads a tree without reading a screen; and `--raw` on an Apple target.
* It is never reported as zero, and it is always the full size. Content-safe gesture bounds are separate.

For Android pixel units and density, see [Android node metadata](#android-node-metadata).

## Presented surface

`snapshot --json` reports `presentedSurface` — whether the capture saw a modal presentation over your app’s own content: `"presented"`, `"absent"`, or `"unknown"`. Read it instead of counting windows in the tree to work out whether a sheet or alert was up.

* `"presented"` means the capture saw the presentation directly — a dimming view, an alert’s own view classes, or an element typed as a sheet, drawer, alert, or dialog.
* `"absent"` is an earned answer, not a default. The capture checked every window it read and each one held only its own content. This is the answer you can act on, for example to confirm a tap dismissed a sheet.
* `"unknown"` means the capture could not tell, and it is not a hedge — it says the capture lacks the evidence absence needs. Absence is only reachable from a capture that reads UIKit class names, so a screen served by a backend that publishes none answers `"unknown"` even when nothing is presented. That is the private accessibility backend (`snapshotQuality.backend: "private-ax"`, which `--actions` asks for) and an Appium tree. Never treat `"unknown"` as `"absent"`.
* A physical iOS device has one capture backend, and it publishes no class names, so there the answer is `"presented"` or `"unknown"` and never `"absent"`.
* The field is absent entirely when the platform publishes no reading at all: Android, web, Linux, and macOS captures.

The answer describes the screen, not the view of it you asked for, so `--raw`, `-i`, `-d`, and `--scope` all report the same value for one screen. Use `-i` or a `--scope` to keep the output small and still trust the answer.

With `--scope`, the text output prints every ref pinned to its ref generation, such as `@e12~s42`, under one `Refs generation: 42` line. Paste the ref as printed into the next command. `--json` and `--raw` keep plain refs.

## iOS capture behavior

Regular iOS snapshots clip overflowing elements to their visible area and omit elements entirely outside it, including system alerts at large text sizes. With `--json`, `snapshotQualityNotes` can include `code: "regular-geometry-clipped"` with `clippedNodeCount` and `droppedNodeCount`. You can continue using visible controls. Use `--raw` to inspect reported frames before clipping.

A regular snapshot that can’t present the screen fails with a typed `details.reason`, such as `regular-node-outside-cumulative-clip`, and `details.index` names the node it refused. One capture gets renumbered along the way, so `details.indexTree` tells you which numbering to read it in:

* `presented` — the tree this command publishes. A passing capture asked the same way lists that node at the same index.
* `acquired` — the tree an unscoped `snapshot --raw` lists, before any clipping.
* `runner-payload` — what the iOS capture published for the request. A passing plain `snapshot` publishes that tree at the same numbers; a passing `snapshot -i` compacts and renumbers it.
* `runner-quality-payload` — a quality-only tree no command lists. Match `details.frame` against a `snapshot --raw` capture to find that node.

iOS snapshots use XCTest on simulators and physical devices. You can’t pick the capture backend. `--raw` switches between two strategies, and each strategy decides which backends it tries.

* Regular (non-`--raw`) capture starts with the XCTest tree. When that comes back **sparse** for a screen XCTest cannot read, it retries with a query sweep and then, on simulators, a private accessibility backend.
* Retries stop when the capture budget runs out, and you get the best result captured so far.
* A failed or partial capture is reported as such instead of looking like an empty UI. A **recovered** capture warns that it fell back to another backend; you can keep working from it. A **sparse** capture reports that no backend could read the screen and points you to `screenshot` plus coordinate taps. Use `--json` and read `snapshotQuality` for the state, backend, and reason behind **degraded** output.
* A **sparse** `snapshot` takes that screenshot for you and returns its path as `fallbackScreenshotPath`, so you don’t need a separate `screenshot` command. Remote clients download the image to the local machine before returning that path. When the screen was reachable but published no accessibility content at all, the warning also names it as a likely app accessibility bug — assistive technologies get the same empty tree. Reasons that describe a limit of this tool instead (a refused or budget-exhausted capture) are not attributed to the app.
* `--raw` starts from the XCTest tree and keeps capture failures strict, so an XCTest accessibility error surfaces as an error instead of an empty tree.
* `--raw` returns the tree as captured, on whichever backend served it. It keeps the off-screen nodes, decorations, and structural wrappers that the default and `-i` views fold away, so a recovered raw capture shows the same hierarchy as a healthy one.
* `-d` still applies with `--raw`, where it counts traversal depth. `-i` narrows only the default view, so `--raw -i` returns the same tree as `--raw`.
* Private-accessibility recovery and `--actions` work on simulators only. Physical iOS devices have no second backend to fall back to.

## Android capture behavior

* Android snapshots need the bundled Android snapshot helper. The first snapshot checks for the helper APK and installs it if it is missing or outdated. If the helper is missing or fails, the error says so directly. In a source checkout, run `pnpm build:android` before verifying on Android.

* On local ADB sessions the helper stays running between captures, and `androidSnapshot.helperTransport` reports `persistent-session`. When that connection isn’t available, the capture retries with a one-shot helper run. Set `AGENT_DEVICE_ANDROID_SNAPSHOT_HELPER_SESSION=0` to turn off the persistent helper.

* When Android exposes them, the helper captures every interactive window, so keyboard and system overlay nodes can appear next to the app’s own tree. `androidSnapshot.captureMode` and `androidSnapshot.windowCount` describe what was captured.

* Regular ADB snapshots clip app rectangles to the visible area outside measured status and navigation bars, including launcher-owned navigation. A partially covered row uses its visible rectangle for taps; content wholly behind a bar is omitted. `--raw` keeps the reported bounds. Ref and selector taps still use the measured visible area when the ref came from a raw snapshot.

* Default and `-i` snapshots keep covered surfaces in the same window visible for diagnosis, and mark controls whose drawing order shows they are covered with `interactionBlocked: "covered"`, so selectors can’t act on a stale React Native screen underneath. Such a node also carries a `coveredBy` description whenever the cover has a name, as [Structured node fields (`--json`)](#structured-node-fields---json) describes.

* Android 6.0 (API 23) doesn’t report the drawing order of sibling views, so this check falls back to conservative behavior there, and `androidSnapshot.occlusionScanUnavailable: true` tells you so.

* `--raw` returns the tree as captured. It also keeps nodes Android marks invisible and stale application windows.

* `--raw` nodes carry four interaction facts that default and `-i` snapshots leave out. An absent field means the capture could not read it, not `false`:

  * `clickable`: the node accepts a tap.
  * `focusable`: keyboard or D-pad focus can land on the node.
  * `longClickable`: the node accepts a long press. Absent when an older snapshot helper served the capture.
  * `scrollable`: the node scrolls its content.

## iOS node metadata

On iOS, React Native controls can report role and state words in `value`, such as `"checkbox, unchecked"`. Snapshot JSON and `get attrs` preserve that value and add `iosValueSemantics` for recognized English encodings from Fabric or Paper. Its `source` is `react-native-ios-value-heuristic`: an anonymous `Other` node with an identical literal value cannot be distinguished from an RN control. Bare words on anonymous nodes, other languages, and native-control values stay uninterpreted.

`iosValueSemantics.role` carries the interpreted role while `type` and native `role` retain their original evidence. Boolean checked state fills a missing `checked` field; an explicit native fact always wins. `iosValueSemantics.checked: "mixed"` never becomes `checked: false`. Read explicit expansion and busy evidence from `iosValueSemantics.expanded` and `.busy`; an absent expansion field means unknown, not collapsed. There is no general `expanded` node field or expansion selector.

## Android node metadata

Android bounds are physical pixels, as the accessibility tree reports them, and so are the points `press`, `fill`, and the gesture commands take. `androidSnapshot.pixelDensity` on a helper capture is the display’s physical pixels per density-independent pixel (a 420 dpi phone reports `2.625`, including any `wm density` override). To work in dp, divide rects by it and multiply your points by it. An older helper omits it. iOS already reports points, so iOS snapshots have no such factor.

`androidSnapshot.missingRootWindowTypes` lists the `AccessibilityWindowInfo` types of windows the helper listed but could not serialize, for example because the window’s root was null or reading its tree failed (`2` is an input method window); `windowCount` counts only the windows it did serialize. It is empty when every listed window was read. When it names an input method window, the capture reports the keyboard band as unmeasurable rather than absent. An older helper omits it.

The response-level `keyboard` field tells you what the capture observed:

* `visible` carries a `frame` observed by the producer in the same coordinates as node bounds. On iOS XCTest, it comes from the capture’s complete pre-projection root snapshot, includes the input assistant bar, and uses the same coordinate normalization as the nodes.
* `derived` carries a `frame` inferred from a docked keyboard tree, with `derivation: "docked-tree"`.
* `visibility-only` carries a boolean `visible` from a provider probe, without a frame.
* `tree-rejected` means the full tree was checked with a usable viewport but could not establish a docked band. Its optional `visible` carries probe visibility. Projecting that tree does not retry the rejected geometry.
* `absent` means the producer explicitly established absence.
* `unmeasurable` carries a `reason` when the producer cannot establish a frame or visibility.

Appium iOS and Android snapshots include a visibility probe. Each capture, including a `wait` poll or the capture before `fill`, adds one sequential probe with a 500 ms timeout. A timeout leaves the probe unknown; it does not discard the tree. Appium iOS can also report a derived docked band during capture. Limrun iOS reports the same keyboard observations as local iOS XCTest. Android Appium can derive the band when a tap resolves the tree’s viewport.

On iOS XCTest, a successful scan of the complete pre-projection root snapshot with no keyboard is the explicit observation that establishes `absent`. A failed or timed-out capture does not establish absence. Missing keyboard nodes in a projected or partial tree never mean the keyboard is hidden. A positive probe establishes presence but cannot locate the covered area. A negative probe establishes absence only when the tree also resolves no docked band. Neither probe result overrides a resolvable docked tree. Element taps use measured or derived frames to refuse an app target whose dispatched tap point is behind the keyboard. Keyboard chrome and app controls hosted on the keyboard surface remain tappable; those app controls still participate in settle observations. Run `snapshot -i` again after ending editing before retrying a refused target.

Android Appium nodes carry the reported native package in `bundleId`. Snapshot nodes can include `keyboardOwned`: `true` means the node belongs to the keyboard tap surface, including app controls hosted there; `false` means capture evaluated the node and found no membership. Both decisions survive filtering and scoping. An omitted field means membership was not evaluated. On native XCTest captures, an `Other` node identified as `SystemInputAssistantView` and its descendants belong to that surface even when the tree has no `Keyboard` node. App controls in the assistant remain part of settle observations.

The Android keyboard band is the input method window’s bounds, the box around the area it takes touches in. On Android 13 (API 33) and later the helper also checks that this area is one rectangle. A floating keyboard’s is not (the panel plus the gesture strip, with app content between them), so the band is reported as unmeasurable and taps fall back to the tree’s own keyboard check. Earlier releases cannot report the area, so their bounds are used as they are.

Android ADB and Appium snapshot nodes carry `systemBar: "status"` or `systemBar: "navigation"` when they belong to a recognized Android system-bar subtree. Membership stays on each node when a snapshot omits its ancestors. The notification shade, including its clock/header, dialogs, popups, and other SystemUI overlays have no bar membership. An absent `systemBar` means the capture did not establish membership. Launcher-hosted navigation buttons carry `"navigation"` too; taskbar app icons do not. Android package identity is available as `bundleId`. You can read these fields in snapshot JSON and nodes returned by `get attrs` and `find`.

Android snapshot nodes and `get attrs` (including the digest response) carry the native `selected`, `checked`, `heading`, `roleDescription`, `editable`, `password`, `hintShowing`, `placeholder`, `selectionStart`, and `selectionEnd` facts whenever the accessibility tree reports them. Explicit `false` and `0` are kept; an absent field means the fact was unavailable, not false. `hintShowing` and `placeholder` need Android API 26 or later, `heading` API 28 or later.

On iOS, the Apple runner publishes native `checked`, `password`, and `editable` facts when available, including on Limrun. The Simulator accessibility bridge and Appium also publish these facts. macOS runner snapshots publish the same native facts.

* `selected` is the accessibility selected state an app sets on a control — the active bottom-tab or segmented-control item, or the chosen row of a list. Android reports it explicitly as `true` or `false`; an older helper APK omits the field, which means the answer is unavailable rather than unselected. Snapshot text marks the node `[selected]`, and `is selected`, a `selected=true` selector, and a Maestro `selected:` qualifier all match on it.
* `checked` is the checked state of a checkable control — a switch, a checkbox, a radio button, or a view an app marked checkable. Android reports it as `true` or `false` on those nodes only; a node that cannot be checked, or an older helper APK, omits the field. Snapshot text marks the node `[checked]` or `[unchecked]`, so a toggle that reads as plain text is one Android did not report as checkable. On iOS and the macOS runner, native switches, checkboxes, radio buttons, and toggles carry `checked` when their native value reports a boolean state; an unavailable or unrecognized state stays absent.
* `editable` is the native text-entry capability when available. `is editable` returns false for a disabled node, even when `editable` is true. Otherwise it uses the published fact, including explicit false, and falls back to the platform type only when the fact is absent. Android Appium leaves `editable` absent when the source does not report it.
* `password` identifies secure text entry. On iOS and the macOS runner, native secure fields report true and ordinary native text-entry fields report false. Android carries the reported native password flag.
* `heading` is the accessibility heading flag an app sets on a node, the way React Native’s `accessibilityRole="header"` does on a plain `View`. The Android helper publishes true for a heading; Appium preserves an explicit true or false when reported. A backend that does not publish this fact leaves it absent.
* `roleDescription` is the localized role description an app sets beside the native class, verbatim (React Native writes `Tab`, `Tab List`, `Radio Group`, `Link`, `Menu`), when the class alone would not say what the control is. The `type` stays the class; a consumer maps the description to a role.
* `value` contains an Android text field’s content, including custom controls that report they are editable. Static labels carry text in `label` and have no `value`. Saved selectors and replay scripts that use `value=` for static labels no longer match; change them to `label=`. `value: ""` means the field reports empty text or `hintShowing: true`; an absent `value` means no field text was reported.
* `placeholder` carries the hint separately, whether the field is empty or filled. A field showing its hint reports `hintShowing: true` and `value: ""`; a field without a hint omits `placeholder`. With Appium, when hint state is unavailable, reported field text is preserved even when it equals the placeholder, and `hintShowing` stays absent. iOS nodes carry the same fact from the field’s `placeholderValue`, on every producer (the XCTest tree, the Simulator AX bridge, and the runner’s private-AX reader). XCTest reports an empty field’s placeholder as its `value` too, so a `value` equal to `placeholder` is either an empty field or one holding exactly that text; equality alone cannot tell them apart.
* `selectionStart`/`selectionEnd` are accessibility selection offsets. They are independent of `editable` (read-only selectable text exposes them too), they are not a character count, and they do not prove that a masked or secure value equals expected text.

# TestMu AI

> Drive TestMu AI (formerly LambdaTest) virtual devices, Android emulators and iOS simulators, and real devices with agent-device.

Use TestMu AI (formerly LambdaTest) to run agent-device on hosted Android emulators, iOS simulators, and real devices over WebDriver. agent-device uses virtual devices (emulators and simulators) by default; pass `--provider-device-type real` for a real device. You need a TestMu AI account and the `@agent-device/testmu` plugin.

## Install the plugin

```bash
agent-device plugins add @agent-device/testmu
```

The plugin is an optional npm package installed under `AGENT_DEVICE_HOME`. After you add or update it, close open sessions and run `agent-device daemon stop` with the state directory you use; the next device command loads the plugin.

## Set credentials and connect

Export your TestMu AI credentials, for example from CI secrets. These are the same variables every TestMu AI SDK reads:

```bash
export LT_USERNAME=...
export LT_ACCESS_KEY=...
```

Connect with the platform, exact device name and OS version, and the app to test:

```bash
export AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION=checkout-android
agent-device connect testmu \
  --platform android \
  --device "Galaxy S22 Ultra 5G" \
  --provider-os-version 14 \
  --provider-app lt://APP-id
```

`--device` and `--provider-os-version` must match the spelling in TestMu AI’s virtual-device catalog exactly. TestMu AI rejects `--provider-os-version 18` for a device listed as `18.0`, so `connect` rejects it too and lists the versions the device offers.

`--provider-app` accepts a TestMu AI app reference such as `lt://APP...`, an HTTP(S) app URL, or an existing local app path (`.apk`, or a zipped simulator `.app` for iOS). When `open` creates the hosted session, agent-device uploads a local path, and TestMu AI fetches a URL, through the virtual-device upload API.

`connect` checks the device/OS pair against TestMu AI’s virtual-device catalog, verifies the credentials against your uploaded-app list, looks up an `lt://` reference in that list, and confirms that a local app file exists before saving its absolute path. A successful `connect` does not prove the app works: it still accepts an `lt://` ID missing from the list, and TestMu AI validates that ID, like a URL or local upload, only when the session starts. `open` takes the app’s installed package or bundle identifier, not the upload name or `lt://` ID.

Optional labels:

```bash
--provider-project agent-device
--provider-build "$GITHUB_RUN_ID"
--provider-session-name "$GITHUB_JOB"
```

Optional device features:

```bash
--provider-device-orientation portrait   # or landscape        (alias --device-orientation)
--provider-geo-location US                                   # (alias --geo-location)
--provider-timezone UTC+05:30                                # (alias --timezone)
--provider-appium-version 2.16.2                             # (alias --appium-version)
--provider-language fr                                       # (alias --language)
--provider-locale fr_FR                                      # (alias --locale)
```

agent-device sends these values to TestMu AI as `lt:options` capabilities when it creates the hosted session.

* Without `--provider-appium-version`, TestMu AI starts its default Appium server for the device. Pin a version when your suite depends on one.
* `--provider-network-profile`, `--provider-custom-network`, and `--provider-no-resign-app` are BrowserStack-only. `connect testmu` and TestMu AI session creation fail with the flag name instead of ignoring them.
* agent-device requests session video and device logs on every session, so `artifacts` has something to return once TestMu AI makes them available.

## Run on real devices

Pass `--provider-device-type real` to run on a physical device. Everything else works as it does for virtual devices: `connect` checks the device/OS pair against the real-device catalog, and agent-device uploads a local path or URL through the real-device upload API.

```bash
export AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION=checkout-real
agent-device connect testmu \
  --provider-device-type real \
  --platform ios \
  --device "iPhone 16" \
  --provider-os-version 18 \
  --provider-app ./MyApp.ipa


agent-device connect testmu \
  --provider-device-type real \
  --platform android \
  --device "Pixel 6" \
  --provider-os-version 14 \
  --provider-app https://example.com/builds/app.apk
```

* Real iOS devices are listed by major OS version only: use `--provider-os-version 18`, not `18.0`. The exact-spelling check still applies, so `connect` rejects `18.0` for a real iPhone 16 and lists the versions it offers.
* Real iOS devices install a signed `.ipa`; a zipped simulator `.app` only runs on simulators. Android takes an `.apk` or `.aab`.
* Real and virtual devices have separate uploads. Pass an `lt://` ID uploaded for the device type you connect to; when in doubt, pass the local path or URL and let agent-device upload it.
* `TESTMU_REAL_DEVICE_APP_UPLOAD_ENDPOINT` redirects real-device uploads, as `TESTMU_APP_UPLOAD_ENDPOINT` does for virtual-device uploads.
* `--provider-device-type` applies only to TestMu AI; BrowserStack, AWS Device Farm, and Limrun refuse it on every route, including `client.leases.allocate()`.

## Run a session from the CLI

```bash
export LT_USERNAME=...
export LT_ACCESS_KEY=...
export AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION=checkout-ios


agent-device connect testmu \
  --platform ios \
  --device "iPhone 16" \
  --provider-os-version 18.0 \
  --provider-app ./MyApp.app.zip \
  --provider-build "$GITHUB_RUN_ID"


agent-device open com.example.app
agent-device snapshot -i
agent-device click 'label="Continue"'
agent-device close
agent-device artifacts --json
agent-device disconnect
```

To drive TestMu AI only through MCP, see [Use a provider only through MCP](/docs/device-clouds#use-a-provider-only-through-mcp).

## Use the Node.js client

The Node.js client reaches TestMu AI through a lease. Allocate one with the provider selectors, then create a client scoped to it for device commands. `sessions.close()` ends the hosted session and releases the lease. Keep `leases.release()` in `finally`: it does nothing after a successful close, and releases the lease when a command fails first. Add `providerDeviceType: 'real'` to `leases.allocate` to run on a real device.

The daemon reads `LT_USERNAME` and `LT_ACCESS_KEY` from its environment, unless a JavaScript host passes the plugin `testmu({ credentials })` instead. If you change credentials while the daemon runs, see [Change credentials while the daemon runs](/docs/device-clouds#change-credentials-while-the-daemon-runs).

```ts
import { createAgentDeviceClient } from 'agent-device';


const scope = {
  tenant: 'testmu',
  runId: process.env.GITHUB_RUN_ID ?? 'local-run',
  leaseBackend: 'ios-instance',
  leaseProvider: 'testmu',
} as const;


const lease = await createAgentDeviceClient().leases.allocate({
  ...scope,
  platform: 'ios',
  device: 'iPhone 16',
  providerOsVersion: '18.0',
  providerApp: 'lt://APP-id',
  providerProject: 'agent-device',
  providerBuild: process.env.GITHUB_RUN_ID,
});
const client = createAgentDeviceClient({ ...scope, leaseId: lease.leaseId });


let providerSessionId: string | undefined;
try {
  await client.apps.open({ app: 'com.example.app' });
  await client.capture.snapshot({ interactiveOnly: true });
  await client.interactions.click({ selector: 'label="Continue"' });
  const closed = await client.sessions.close();
  providerSessionId = closed.provider?.providerSessionId;
} finally {
  await client.leases.release({ ...scope, leaseId: lease.leaseId });
}


if (providerSessionId) {
  const artifacts = await client.sessions.artifacts({ provider: 'testmu', providerSessionId });
  if ('cloudArtifacts' in artifacts) console.log(artifacts.cloudArtifacts);
}
```

## Get artifacts and troubleshoot

After `close`, TestMu AI can return session video, Appium logs, device logs, network and command logs, a screenshot archive, and the App Automation dashboard link. The provider session ID is the WebDriver session ID. See [Retrieve artifacts after close](/docs/device-clouds#retrieve-artifacts-after-close).

To use a staging or private TestMu AI deployment, redirect the WebDriver, upload, and catalog/session-detail endpoints with `TESTMU_WEBDRIVER_ENDPOINT`, `TESTMU_APP_UPLOAD_ENDPOINT` (virtual devices), `TESTMU_REAL_DEVICE_APP_UPLOAD_ENDPOINT` (real devices), and `TESTMU_API_ENDPOINT`. The app list that `connect` uses to check credentials always comes from `https://manual-api.lambdatest.com/app/data`.

To enter text, see [Fill text on hosted WebDriver sessions](/docs/device-clouds#fill-text-on-hosted-webdriver-sessions).

# Samsung Tizen

> Drive web apps on Samsung Tizen TVs with agent-device through sdb and the Chrome DevTools Protocol.

Use the `@agent-device/tizen` plugin to drive web apps on Samsung Tizen TVs. The plugin debug-launches the app over `sdb`, forwards its DevTools port, and drives the page over the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP): remote keys, pointer, text, snapshots, screenshots, and console logs.

The plugin is experimental. The commands it admits are listed in [How commands map to the TV](#how-commands-map-to-the-tv).

## Requirements

* `sdb` from the Tizen SDK of the VS Code Tizen extension, set up with its Set Up step. The plugin finds it in the SDK that `$TIZEN_SDK` or `~/.tizen.path.config` names. `sdb` is not on `PATH`; to point at it directly, set the `sdbPath` plugin option.
* The TV in Developer Mode with this host’s IP set as the developer IP. To set this up, follow Samsung’s [Connecting the TV and SDK](https://developer.samsung.com/smarttv/develop/getting-started/using-sdk/tv-device.html).
* The app installed on the TV from a debug-enabled package.
* The TV and this host on the same network.

## Install the plugin

```bash
agent-device plugins add @agent-device/tizen
```

The plugin is an optional npm package installed under `AGENT_DEVICE_HOME`. After you add or update it, close open sessions and run `agent-device daemon stop` with the state directory you use; the next device command loads the plugin.

Plugin options, set under `plugins["@agent-device/tizen"].options` in `config.json`:

| Option    | Meaning                                                                                             |
| --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `sdbPath` | Path to `sdb`, when the Tizen SDK is not found.                                                     |
| `device`  | TV IP or sdb serial to drive when `connect` names none. Defaults to the only TV connected to `sdb`. |

## Connect and run a session

```bash
export AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION=checkout-tv
agent-device connect tizen --device 192.0.2.10
agent-device open com.example.app
agent-device wait text "Home"
agent-device tv-remote press down
agent-device snapshot -i
agent-device screenshot ./tv.png
agent-device logs start
agent-device close com.example.app
agent-device disconnect
```

The TV is a leased device, so every command from `connect` to `disconnect` names its session with `AGENT_DEVICE_SESSION`, `--session <name>`, or a config session. Without one, the command fails with `REMOTE_SESSION_REQUIRED`.

`--device` takes the TV IP or an sdb serial. When the TV is not connected to `sdb` yet, the plugin runs `sdb connect <ip>:26101`. Without `--device`, the plugin uses the `device` option, then the only TV connected to `sdb`. `connect` does not contact the TV; `open` connects it.

agent-device leases only iOS, Android, and HarmonyOS devices, so a Tizen TV enters as an Android TV device that the plugin owns (`platform: android`, `target: tv`, id `tizen:<sdb serial>`). Every command on that device goes to the plugin, never to adb.

## How commands map to the TV

| Command                                                                                                                        | How                                                                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `open` / `close`                                                                                                               | `sdb shell 0 was_kill`, `sdb shell 0 debug`, and `sdb forward`, then CDP / `sdb shell 0 was_kill`                                                                   |
| `tv-remote press up/down/left/right/select/back`, `back`                                                                       | `Input.dispatchKeyEvent` with the Samsung remote codes                                                                                                              |
| `tv-remote press media-play/media-pause/media-play-pause/media-stop/media-next/media-previous/media-rewind/media-fast-forward` | `Input.dispatchKeyEvent` with the Samsung media key codes                                                                                                           |
| `appstate`                                                                                                                     | The attached app while its page is visible                                                                                                                          |
| `apps`                                                                                                                         | `sdb shell 0 vd_applist`                                                                                                                                            |
| `logs`                                                                                                                         | Console calls, exceptions, and browser log entries of the attached page, one line each                                                                              |
| `snapshot`, `find`, `is`, `get`, `wait`                                                                                        | A DOM walk over `Runtime.evaluate`: visible interactive, labelled, or text nodes, with focus from `document.activeElement`. `-s`, `-d`, and `-i` apply to the walk. |
| `screenshot`                                                                                                                   | `Page.captureScreenshot`. `--crop-on <selector>` crops the capture to the frame of the node that the selector resolves in a snapshot taken on the same screen.      |
| `click`, `press <x> <y>`, `longpress`, `hover`                                                                                 | `Input.dispatchMouseEvent`                                                                                                                                          |
| `fill`                                                                                                                         | Pointer press on the field, select its contents, then `Input.insertText`, or Backspace for an empty value                                                           |
| `type`                                                                                                                         | `Input.insertText` into the focused element                                                                                                                         |
| `scroll`                                                                                                                       | `mouseWheel` at the centre of the scroll container or the viewport, by the requested distance                                                                       |

Not supported yet: system buttons (`home`, menu, volume, and channel), `network dump`, `perf`, `install` and `uninstall`, recording, URLs and deep links in `open`, and `power`.

## Known limitations

* `open` is always a cold start: `sdb shell 0 debug` cannot attach to a running app, so `open` kills it first. `open` can return before the app leaves its splash screen; wait for app content before the first snapshot.
* Idle leases expire after 60 seconds by default, and expiry ends the session. When the lease ends, by `disconnect` or by expiry, the plugin closes the page connection and removes the `sdb` forward. The next command then fails with `Lease is not active` or `No active session` and needs a new `connect` and `open`. To keep longer pauses alive, run `agent-device daemon stop`, then start the daemon with `AGENT_DEVICE_LEASE_TTL_MS` and `AGENT_DEVICE_LEASE_MAX_TTL_MS` set, for example `1800000`.
* `screenshot` captures the app page, not the TV screen. When the app is in the background, the page renders no frames, so `screenshot` fails; `open <appId>` brings the app back. While the on-screen keyboard is open, the page viewport and the screenshot are shorter. System layers such as the Samsung menu never appear in `screenshot` or `snapshot`.
* `appstate` knows only the attached app. The TV reports no foreground app that the plugin can read.
* Console messages logged before the attach are replayed without object previews.
* A second DevTools client on the same page can hang the session. Close Chrome DevTools and other inspector clients attached to the app first.
* Snapshots are read from the DOM. Labels come from `aria-label`, `alt`, `title`, or own text. Rects are CSS pixels. The screenshot magnifies them by the page’s `visualViewport.scale`: a `width=1280` meta viewport on a 1920x1080 TV gives 1.5. `screenshot --crop-on` applies that scale, and refuses a page whose browser has no `visualViewport` or whose visual viewport is panned. `screenshot --overlay-refs` draws ref boxes at the same scale; without one it draws them 1:1. The walk does not enter iframes or shadow roots.

# LG webOS

> Drive web apps on LG webOS TVs with agent-device through the webOS CLI and the Chrome DevTools Protocol.

Use the `@agent-device/webos` plugin to drive web apps on LG webOS TVs. The plugin launches the app with the webOS CLI, opens the `ares-inspect` tunnel, and drives the page over the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP): remote keys, pointer, text, snapshots, screenshots, and console logs.

The plugin is experimental. The commands it admits are listed in [How commands map to the TV](#how-commands-map-to-the-tv).

## Requirements

* The webOS CLI (`ares-*`) on `PATH`, or the directory that holds it passed as the `aresBin` plugin option. To install it, follow LG’s [webOS CLI installation](https://webostv.developer.lge.com/develop/tools/cli-installation).
